Buoyed by strong local demand and improved export performance, Hong Kong's economy maintained robust growth momentum in the second half of 2017. Economic growth is projected to remain robust in 2018. However, the economic outlook for Hong Kong continues to be influenced by numerous uncertainties and risks, including the normalization of monetary policies by major central banks, stability concerns in global financial markets, rising protectionist sentiments, and escalating geopolitical tensions. In the short term, while local inflationary pressures are expected to remain moderate, certain upside risks persist. Hong Kong's economy maintained its growth momentum in the second half of 2017. Seasonally adjusted real gross domestic product (GDP) grew at a quarterly rate of 0.8% in both the third and fourth quarters, comparable to the average quarterly growth rate of 0.9% in the preceding two quarters (Figure 3.1). Compared with the first half of the year, private consumption continued to grow robustly and remained a key driver of GDP growth. This robust consumption growth was underpinned by sound employment and income conditions, sustained consumer optimism, and positive wealth effects arising from rising asset prices. Although building and construction activities weakened, increased corporate capital expenditure led to a significant rise in overall investment spending in the final quarter, following three quarters of broadly stable performance. On the external front, Hong Kong's export performance improved further, benefiting from stronger global trade growth and a gradual recovery in inbound tourism (Figure 3.2). Nevertheless, as the growth rate of imports outpaced that of exports, net exports of goods continued to drag on GDP growth, while net exports of services made a positive contribution. Figure 3.1 Growth Rate of Real GDP and Contributions of Major Expenditure Components; Figure 3.2 Real Exports and Imports. Sustained economic growth momentum drove an increase in employment in the second half of 2017. During the period, total employment rose by approximately 0.7% to over 3.85 million, with the most significant increases recorded in the construction, financial and business services, and public administration, social and personal services sectors. As the growth in real GDP outpaced the growth in employment, there were signs of further improvement in labour productivity. Economic growth is expected to remain robust in 2018. On the external front, Hong Kong's export performance is projected to continue benefiting from an improved global economic outlook and a gradual recovery in inbound tourism. Locally, private consumption is expected to continue growing, primarily due to favourable labour market conditions. Given that Hong Kong dollar interest rates will eventually rise, Topic 3 examines the impact of higher mortgage repayment burdens on private consumption. Regarding domestic fixed capital formation, building and construction activities are expected to grow steadily, benefiting from increased housing supply and the ongoing rollout of infrastructure projects. While an improving economic environment will stimulate corporate capital expenditure, potential interest rate hikes could exert a negative impact. The Government projects real GDP growth for 2018 to be in the range of 3% to 4%, while growth forecasts from international institutions and private sector analysts range between 2% and 4%. However, Hong Kong's growth outlook remains subject to numerous uncertainties and risks, including the external environment, mainland China's economic performance amid tightening financial conditions, and trends in local asset markets, as mentioned in earlier chapters. Local inflationary pressures remained contained in the second half of 2017, though there were signs of a slight pickup in inflation momentum in recent months. On a year-on-year basis, the Core Consumer Price Index (CPI) rose by 1.7% and 1.6% in the third and fourth quarters respectively, comparable to the average increase of about 1.7% in the first half of the year. However, the core inflation rate, which reflects inflation momentum and is calculated on a three-month annualized basis, edged up slightly to 2.8% in January 2018 (Figure 3.3). Prices for both tradables and services increased. The recovery in newly signed private residential rents since mid-2016 may also have contributed to some extent to the inflation momentum (Figure 3.4). Furthermore, labour cost pressures have remained moderate in recent quarters (Figure 3.5). Figure 3.3 Various Indicators Reflecting Consumer Price Inflation; Figure 3.4 CPI Rent Component and Market Rents; Figure 3.5 Unit Labour Costs and Average Earnings per Employee. Given that global inflation remains moderate and local cost increases are stable, inflationary pressures in Hong Kong are expected to remain moderate in 2018, although the core inflation rate may gradually recover from its eight-year low of 1.7% in 2017. For instance, inflationary pressures may increase in the second half of 2018 due to the pass-through effect from the growth in newly signed private residential rents. Market consensus forecasts an overall inflation rate of a moderate 2.2% for 2018, while the Government's forecast for the core inflation rate is 2.5%. Although the inflation outlook is moderate, upside risks remain. On the external front, if global inflation or commodity prices record higher-than-expected increases, local inflation momentum could rise. Locally, the labour market has tightened further recently, with the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate falling from 3.4% in 2016 to 2.9% in December 2017, dropping below 3% for the first time in nearly 20 years (Figure 3.6). The current output gap is estimated to be close to zero; should the labour market tighten significantly, it could exert additional upward pressure on inflation. Figure 3.6 Unemployment Rate. Following the 2008 global financial crisis, low interest rates led to an increase in mortgage indebtedness among Hong Kong households. As the normalization of US dollar interest rates progresses, Hong Kong dollar interest rates will eventually follow suit, leading to a corresponding increase in future household mortgage repayment burdens, thereby dragging on household consumption. Therefore, this topic examines the impact of increased mortgage repayment burdens on private consumption in Hong Kong. The mortgage repayment burden refers to the ratio of mortgage debt service payments (i.e., interest payments plus principal amortization) to income. Figure B3.1 illustrates the role of the mortgage repayment burden in the transmission of interest rate shocks to private consumption. In addition to the substitution effect, income effect, wealth effect, and collateral effect induced by asset price changes mentioned in general economic theory, interest rate shocks also affect private consumption by altering mortgage interest payments in the presence of a mortgage repayment burden, thereby changing household disposable income. This impact will expand with an increase in the outstanding mortgage loan balance. Moreover, the principal amortization amount varies with changes in the outstanding mortgage loan balance, which also affects private consumption through changes in household disposable income. Figure B3.1 Determinants of Private Consumption. To measure the impact of the mortgage repayment burden on private consumption, we estimated the Outstanding Mortgage Debt Service-to-Income Ratio (OMDSR) based on outstanding mortgage liabilities. Unlike the existing mortgage repayment burden indicator which applies only to new mortgage liabilities, OMDSR covers the overall outstanding mortgage liabilities of all households, which are more closely related to total private consumption. Following the methodology used by the Bank for International Settlements, we measured OMDSR using the standard formula for fixed installments: where Dt is the outstanding residential mortgage loan amount in the banking sector, Yt is the total income of owner-occupier households (measured by the median income of owner-occupier households multiplied by the number of such households), and rt and st are the average interest rate and tenure of outstanding mortgage loans, respectively. To assess whether OMDSR reliably measures the mortgage repayment burden for the entire household sector, it is appropriate to compare OMDSR with two commonly used burden indicators. Figure B3.2 shows the estimated OMDSR from 1985 to 2017, alongside the median debt service-to-income ratio estimated by the Census and Statistics Department based on the quinquennial population census. In the early 2000s, both ratios exhibited a downward trend, consistent with the overall reduction in household mortgage borrowing and the sharp decline in mortgage interest rates following the bursting of the property bubble in 1997. Despite the substantial rise in property prices after the global financial crisis, these two ratios remained stable, attributable to the Hong Kong Monetary Authority's (HKMA) macro-prudential measures on bank mortgage lending, which curbed overall household mortgage leverage. Additionally, the extension of tenures for new mortgage loans also reduced the actual amount of mortgage payments. Figure B3.2 OMDSR and Median Debt Service-to-Income Ratio. We also compared OMDSR with the banks' debt service-to-income (DSI) ratio, which represents the actual DSI ratio of new mortgage applicants to banks. As shown in Figure B3.3, OMDSR is lower than the banks' DSI ratio, partly because OMDSR covers not only new mortgages but also existing ones. Since existing mortgages were established when property prices were lower, their payments correspondingly are lower than those of new mortgages. Therefore, the outstanding mortgage repayment burden indicator covering both existing and new mortgages (i.e., OMDSR) is lower than the burden indicator for new mortgages (i.e., the banks' DSI ratio). Furthermore, the higher banks' DSI ratio is also due to banks complying with the HKMA's prudential regulatory requirements by including non-mortgage loan repayments in the DSI calculation. Following the global financial crisis, both OMDSR and the banks' DSI ratio remained stable, primarily due to the HKMA's implementation of prudential regulation on mortgage lending, which set caps on banks' DSI ratios; this measure also helped to dampen OMDSR. Figure B3.3 OMDSR and Banks' DSI Ratio for New Mortgages. Overall, OMDSR is broadly consistent with commonly used burden indicators, but OMDSR possesses greater timeliness and can reflect the burden of the entire outstanding mortgage debt, not just new mortgage liabilities. Therefore, we believe that using OMDSR allows for an assessment of the impact of the mortgage repayment burden on private consumption. To evaluate this impact on private consumption in Hong Kong, we estimated an error-correction model following the methods of Lai and Lam (2002) and Kang (2016). In this model, the long-run relationship between real private consumption (measured by real average private consumption per household) and its determinants is represented in the short-run equation by an error-correction term. Based on existing theory and empirical evidence, we identified real income (measured by median household income, deflated by the CPI), real housing and financial wealth (measured respectively by residential property prices and the Hang Seng Index, deflated by the CPI), and OMDSR as the long-run determinants of private consumption.

As the tight HKD liquidity conditions eased and year-end commercial demand for US dollars rose, the HKD spot exchange rate weakened again in mid-December 2017. Entering 2018, despite increased volatility in global financial markets (particularly equity markets), the HKD continued to operate in an orderly manner. Bank credit grew strongly throughout 2017. The loan growth rate was as high as 10.2% in the first half and slowed to 5.3% in the second half (Figure 4.10). Driven primarily by growth in net interest income, the profitability of retail banks improved in the second half of 2017 compared with the same period in 2016. Despite a significant rise in the Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate (HIBOR), the cost of HKD funding for retail banks remained low due to persistently low retail deposit rates.
