To address the potentially severe economic impact of the pandemic, some central banks (including the US Federal Reserve, the Bank of Canada, and the Bank of England) cut interest rates since early March, while some governments introduced targeted measures to support households and businesses. However, financial markets still face significant selling pressure, leading to a notable tightening of global financial conditions, which may in turn exacerbate downward pressure on the global economy (Figure 2.4). Figure 2.4 Bloomberg Advanced Economies Financial Conditions Index. Besides the development of the pandemic, other downside risks and uncertainties also loom over the global economic outlook. Particularly regarding trade tensions, although policy risks have declined following the first phase US-China trade agreement, subsequent negotiations may prove difficult due to numerous unresolved structural issues. In Europe, trade negotiations between the EU and the UK are expected to be challenging, thereby prolonging uncertainties post-Brexit. Additionally, the sharp decline in oil prices since March will exert pressure on major oil-exporting emerging economies. In East Asia, real economic activity remained sluggish in the second half of 2019 due to low global demand. Regional exports to major destinations such as the United States, European economies, and mainland China remained weak in the second half of 2019 (Figure 2.5). Although there are preliminary signs that the downturn cycle for regional technology products is bottoming out and recovering—including reports from major regional electronics companies of improved earnings at the end of 2019—whether a substantive rebound in regional technology product exports will materialize remains to be seen. Figure 2.5 East Asia: Commodity Exports to Major Destinations Remain Weak. Persistent weak economic growth and trade uncertainties have also dampened investor sentiment, leading to a decline in total gross fixed capital formation in most East Asian economies in 2019 (Figure 2.6), which could affect the region's potential economic growth in the long run. To support economic growth in an environment of moderate inflation, the central banks of Indonesia, the Philippines, and South Korea lowered policy rates again in the second half of 2019 after cutting rates in the first half, while the Bank of Thailand also lowered its policy rate for the first time since 2015. Figure 2.6 East Asia: Total Gross Fixed Capital Formation. The coronavirus outbreak has raised concerns that regional economies may face further pressure amid persistently weak growth. As multiple regional economies have implemented entry and exit restrictions on mainland China, the tourism sector has been hit first and foremost; economies more reliant on mainland Chinese tourists and tourism service exports have been more severely affected by this outbreak (Figure 2.7). The continuation and intensification of the pandemic will also affect regional supply chains closely linked with mainland China. Figure 2.7 East Asia: Tourism Exports and Chinese Tourists. In the short term, this pandemic will continue to affect economic activity and investor sentiment. Drawing on the experience of the 2003 SARS outbreak, these impacts may be temporary, but the actual situation will depend on the severity and spread of the pandemic, as well as the effectiveness of government actions to contain the outbreak. Meanwhile, East Asian economies also face multiple headwinds. First, although market expectations indicate that corporate earnings will deteriorate in the short term (Figure 2.8), globally accommodative monetary conditions encourage yield-seeking activities, thereby pushing up asset prices without fundamental support. Consequently, regional stock markets are more susceptible to shifts in investor sentiment. Figure 2.8 Expected Earnings of Benchmark Stock Index Constituents. Second, weak corporate earnings and economic growth may make it more difficult for private sector entities in the region to service their debts. Although declining local interest rates can provide some breathing room for indebted companies and households, they may also sow the seeds for further debt accumulation. Furthermore, as noted in Feature 1, as more index-tracking funds flow into regional financial markets, the risk of debt buildup among private sector entities may intensify, although this impact may be limited to firms with sounder financial fundamentals and their long-term borrowing. Third, regarding external factors, facing increasingly protectionist US trade policies, the risks faced by East Asian economies may also increase. Despite recent progress in the first phase US-China trade agreement, fundamental trade issues between the two countries remain, and US-China trade tensions persist. As evidenced by the continuously rising trade surpluses of multiple regional economies with the United States (Figure 2.9), multinational corporations may continue to seek more supply channels outside China-centric supply chains to evade tariffs. As of November 2019, the cumulative trade surplus of nine Asian emerging economies (excluding China) with the United States had increased to approximately USD 167 billion. If trade surpluses with the United States continue to expand, relevant Asian economies may become the next targets of trade wars; for example, the US government imposed tariffs as high as 456% on Vietnamese steel imports in July 2019. In light of this, despite the US-China trade truce, the regional trade outlook remains highly uncertain. Figure 2.9 Goods Trade Surplus with the United States. Over the past decade, intensified integration of international financial markets has significantly increased global cross-border securities investment flows. A recent study shows that up to 70% of these cross-border investment flows are driven by index-driven funds. Index-driven funds include not only funds that closely track investment indices (commonly known as passive funds) but also funds that actively manage portfolios while referencing investment indices. By introducing overseas investors that relevant economies could not previously attract or access, these funds have helped develop the financial markets of emerging market economies. Consequently, such funds enable emerging market economies to diversify their investor base, contributing to long-term market growth and stability. However, is there really such a thing as a free lunch? Regarding passive bond funds, market concerns exist that such investments may weaken the fiscal discipline of the corporate bond issuers they invest in, thereby leading to elevated leverage levels for those enterprises. Additionally, it is argued that the growth of index-driven funds in recent years has exacerbated the volatility of global securities investment flows, making emerging market economies—which are already highly sensitive to global factors and influenced by other common factors—even more vulnerable. This feature evaluates the impact of index-driven investment on financial stability with respect to these two propositions. Passive bond funds allocate their investment capital to relevant bonds according to the weights of constituent bonds within the benchmark index. Therefore, compared to actively managed bond funds, the mechanical investment decisions adopted by passive bond funds may reduce the incentives for issuers of index constituent bonds to act in the interests of fund investors. Worse still, from a financial stability perspective, such behavior may encourage excessive borrowing, bringing significant credit and solvency risks to the corporate sector of emerging market economies, whose leverage ratios have risen sharply since the global financial crisis (Figure B1.1). Figure B1.1 Corporate Leverage in Emerging Market Economies. Using the weights of enterprises in emerging market economies within a mainstream index tracking emerging market corporate bonds as an estimate of their bonds' exposure to investment by passive bond funds, we find that an increase in such investments will raise the long-term (rather than short-term) leverage ratios of the relevant corporate bond issuers. The blue solid bars in Figure B1.2 indicate the estimated impact. In addition to promoting the development of the corporate bond market in emerging market economies, the expanded base of long-term bond investors due to passive bond funds also benefits the development of enterprises in emerging market economies. We also find that the aforementioned effects have a significant impact only on enterprises in emerging market economies with stronger fundamentals (particularly stronger solvency and lower leverage ratios) (green solid bars in Figure B1.2). Facing higher costs of financial distress, highly leveraged or less solvent enterprises do not seem to fall further into debt traps due to investment by passive bond funds. In summary, the above research indicates that the growth of passive bond fund investments does not necessarily substantially increase solvency risks for the corporate sector of emerging market economies.

Driven by weaker private consumption, reduced investment expenditure, and poor export performance, Hong Kong's economy contracted in the second half of 2019, entering its first recession since 2009. Economic performance in 2020 is expected to face significant challenges, with the recent coronavirus outbreak introducing substantial downside risks. The economic outlook is influenced by numerous uncertainties and risks, including slowing global economic growth, the US-China trade relationship, mainland China's economic performance, and the evolution of local social events. Given these various headwinds, the unemployment rate is likely to rise further in 2020. While domestic inflationary pressures are expected to ease, the outlook faces potential risks from both the upside and the downside. Hong Kong's economy contracted significantly in the second half of 2019. On a year-on-year basis, real gross domestic product (GDP) contracted by 2.8% in the third quarter and 2.9% in the fourth quarter (Table 3.A). Dragged down by the contraction in the second half of the year, the economy shrank by 1.2% for the full year, a deterioration from the 2.9% growth recorded in 2018, and marking the first annual contraction since the 2009 global financial crisis. Figure 3.1: Growth Rate of Real GDP and Contributions of Major Expenditure Components. On a quarter-on-quarter basis, economic activity slowed significantly in the second half of the year (Figure 3.1). Specifically, real GDP fell by 0.4%, 3.0%, and 0.3% in the second, third, and fourth quarters respectively, indicating that the economy had entered a recession. Domestically, private consumption was the primary factor dragging down GDP in the third quarter. Local social events severely impacted consumption activities, weakening the economic outlook and undermining consumer confidence, leading to a significant contraction in private consumption starting in the third quarter. Due to increased economic uncertainties and a deteriorating business sentiment, total investment expenditure remained weak and weighed on GDP in the fourth quarter. Externally, amid escalating US-China trade tensions, weakening global economic growth, and a sharp decline in visitor arrivals, Hong Kong's external trade performance continued to be sluggish (Figure 3.2). Under the influence of a sharp contraction in services exports, net exports dragged down GDP in the third quarter but provided support for GDP growth in the fourth quarter, partly reflecting an improvement in the merchandise trade balance. Figure 3.2: Real Exports and Imports. Given the significant headwinds facing the economy, the government launched multiple rounds of measures between August and December 2019 to alleviate the financial burden on residents, safeguard employment, and support businesses, particularly small and medium enterprises (SMEs) and severely impacted sectors such as retail, food and beverage services, transportation, and tourism. To give banks greater room to intensify their support for the local economy and help moderate the economic cycle, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) announced on October 14 a reduction in the countercyclical capital buffer ratio for banks from 2.5% to 2.0%. This would enable banks to release an additional lending capacity of HKD 200 billion to 300 billion to businesses, including SMEs. Economic performance in Hong Kong in 2020 is expected to face significant challenges, with the recent pandemic introducing substantial downside risks. Since some sectors have yet to recover from the damage caused by social events, the pandemic will deliver a double blow to these sectors. However, a series of countercyclical measures announced in the 2020-21 Budget can provide assistance to households and businesses (particularly SMEs), including a one-off cash handout to adult permanent residents and preferential low-interest loans with 100% government guarantee under the SME Financing Guarantee Scheme for businesses. On March 16, 2020, the HKMA further reduced the countercyclical capital buffer ratio for banks from 2.0% to 1.0%, providing banks with greater room to intensify support for the local economy, especially for sectors and individuals facing increased pressure in the short term due to the pandemic. Analyzing the components of GDP, private consumption and investment are likely to remain weak due to fragile consumption and business confidence. While government consumption will support economic growth, public investment expenditure is expected to remain relatively subdued as some major infrastructure projects are completed. Regarding external factors, the first phase of the US-China trade agreement is expected to have a slight positive impact on the local economy in the short term. However, weak global economic growth and trade activity will continue to drag down Hong Kong's external trade performance. In particular, the coronavirus outbreak may lead to disruptions in regional supply chains and a slowdown in cross-border economic activities (such as tourism), thereby limiting Hong Kong's export performance. The government forecasts real GDP growth for 2020 to be between -1.5% and 0.5%, while the average growth forecast from international institutions and private sector analysts is -1.5%. This weak economic outlook is influenced by the numerous uncertainties and risks described in previous chapters. The labor market faced greater pressure in the second half of 2019 and the early months of 2020. The seasonally adjusted unemployment rate rose from a multi-year low of 2.8% in June 2019 to 3.3% in December 2019, and further climbed to 3.7% in February 2020 (Figure 3.3). Among these, the unemployment rate in the retail, accommodation, and food and beverage services sectors surged to a near-decade high of 6.1%, partly reflecting the severe impact of social events. As economic momentum weakened, the total number of employed persons fell by 0.5% year-on-year in the second half of 2019 and continued to decline to 3,768,800 in February 2020. The decline in employment was mainly driven by the trade, wholesale, retail, accommodation, food and beverage services, and construction sectors. Real wages also fell by 0.3% year-on-year in the third quarter. Looking ahead, in light of the aforementioned weak economic outlook, the labor market will continue to face more challenges, and the unemployment rate is very likely to rise further. Feature 3 will explore recent developments and the short-term outlook for the labor market in greater detail. Figure 3.3: Labor Market Conditions. Domestic inflationary pressures continued to accumulate until the third quarter of 2019, mainly due to rising prices of fresh pork; subsequently, as economic activity weakened, inflationary momentum gradually slowed. On a year-on-year basis, the Core Composite Consumption Price Index (CPI) grew by 3.3% in the third quarter, with the growth rate easing slightly to 3.0% in the fourth quarter. The Core Inflation Rate, calculated on a three-month annualized basis to reflect inflationary momentum, also softened from a high of 4.7% in August 2019 to 2.1% in January 2020. The easing of inflationary momentum was due to reduced price pressures on multiple components of the CPI. Regarding tradable goods, rising fresh pork prices kept core food inflation notable, although price pressures on consumer goods such as clothing and footwear and durable goods remained moderate. Regarding services, with the growth in newly signed private residential rents slowing down, the growth in the rent component of the CPI also showed a downward trend (Figure 3.5). Labor cost pressures rose slightly but remained at a moderate level in recent quarters (Figure 3.6). Figure 3.4: Different Indicators Reflecting CPI Inflation. Figure 3.5: Rent Component of the Composite CPI and Market Rents. Figure 3.6: Unit Labor Costs. Domestic inflationary pressures are expected to ease in the short term. Domestically, weak economic conditions and a widening negative output gap will continue to exert downward pressure on local inflation. With private residential rents continuing to slow, the housing rent component of inflation should further moderate. Externally, due to weak global economic growth and soft energy prices, import inflation is expected to remain moderate. Market consensus forecasts the overall inflation rate for 2020 to be between 0.6% and 3.7%, while the government forecasts a core inflation rate of 2.5% and an overall inflation rate of 1.7%. This inflation outlook is influenced by risk factors from both the upside and the downside. On the one hand, given that the estimated negative output gap has widened since the third quarter of 2019, if the economic deterioration is more severe than expected (for example, due to the persistence of the coronavirus outbreak), inflation may be further suppressed. On the other hand, if the disruption to fresh pork supplies becomes more severe, it will bring upward pressure on inflation. Although the local economy slowed significantly, the unemployment rate remained at a low level of 2.8%-2.9% during the first nine months of 2019. It was only with the continuation of social events that the unemployment rate rose more noticeably to 3.3% by the end of 2019. Affected by the coronavirus outbreak, the labor market will face greater resistance in 2020. Against this backdrop, this feature analyzes recent developments and the short-term outlook for the labor market, including exploring why the overall labor market remained relatively robust in the first three quarters of 2019 (with almost no change in the unemployment rate) and what implications this has for future developments. This paper also examines some risk factors that could lead to a sharp rise in the unemployment rate. It is worth noting that, partly due to the costs of adjusting labor demand, the unemployment rate is a lagging indicator. In fact, the unemployment rate often lags the year-on-year growth rate of real GDP by about two to three quarters (Figure B3.1). This lagging nature explains why the unemployment rate remained low at around 2.9% when real economic activity deteriorated sharply in the third quarter. Figure B3.1: Real GDP Growth Rate and Unemployment Rate. Regarding labor demand, although the tense US-China trade situation and local social events dealt heavy blows to employment in the trade and retail/tourism-related sectors respectively, some major sectors were still able to support the overall labor market. Specifically, employment in finance, business services, public administration, and social and personal services continued to grow in 2019, partially offsetting the decline in employment in the trade and retail sectors (Figure B3.2). Despite the economy entering a recession, Hong Kong's financial system remained robust, and financial activities in fintech development and initial public offerings were very active. These factors may help support the employment market in the finance and business services sectors. Furthermore, public administration, social, and personal services, including education, healthcare, and social work activities, appear to be less sensitive to the economic cycle. Correlation analysis shows that while employment in many sectors is highly correlated with real GDP, public administration, social, and personal services respond more neutrally to the economic cycle. In other words, even if the economy slows down, employment in these sectors may not be significantly affected by cyclical factors. Figure B3.2: Changes in Employment by Sector in 2019. Regarding labor supply, the labor force participation rate fell from 61.2% in 2018 to 60.5% in 2019, providing a buffer for the rise in unemployment. Figure B3.3 shows the various supply and demand factors influencing changes in the unemployment rate (blue line). As shown in the chart, the labor force participation rate (green bars) exerted downward pressure on the unemployment rate in 2019. On the other hand, the increase in the number of employed persons in the first half of 2019 (purple bars) also helped suppress the unemployment rate. However, with a significant economic contraction in the second half of the year, the decline in employment exerted upward pressure on the unemployment rate. Overall, although employment declined during the recession, the lower labor force participation rate helped alleviate the pressure on the rising unemployment rate in the second half of 2019. Figure B3.3: Factors Leading to Changes in the Unemployment Rate. Some structural changes in the labor market are also worth noting. In particular, an increase in the proportion of voluntary part-time employees may help companies retain staff. In fact, while the proportions of self-employed persons and underemployed persons in total employment have declined in recent years to 6% and 1% respectively, the number of voluntary part-time employees has continued to rise, becoming the second-largest group in the total employed population (around 7% in 2017). Therefore, companies may retain or hire more employees by adjusting the working hours of part-time staff. Our calculations show that the average weekly working hours have decreased, falling from a recent high of 48 hours in 2010 to approximately 44 hours currently, partly reflecting a higher proportion of part-time workers in the current employed population.

The Hong Kong dollar (HKD) exchange rate has strengthened since October, with upward momentum intensifying in December, keeping the HKD consistently at the strong end of the exchange rate band over the past few months. Strong demand for the HKD stems partly from equity-related demand and partly from the unwinding of short HKD positions driven by liquidity tightening towards year-end. Overall, Hong Kong's foreign exchange and currency markets have continued to operate smoothly and in an orderly manner. Although market sentiment triggered by the coronavirus outbreak in an uncertain external environment may exacerbate capital flow volatility, Hong Kong's substantial foreign exchange reserves and robust banking system enable it to withstand capital outflow pressures without compromising local financial stability. Supported by increased equity-related demand for the HKD, including initial public offerings (IPOs), the HKD exchange rate has gradually strengthened since mid-October (Figure 4.1). In December, upward momentum further intensified, with the HKD remaining at the strong end of the exchange rate band from mid-December through February. The strengthening of the HKD was partly due to robust IPO activity and partly due to the unwinding of short HKD positions triggered by liquidity tightening towards year-end. Following the Lunar New Year holiday, liquidity conditions eased, and the HKD exchange rate softened slightly, closing at 7.7956 on 28 February. Overall, HKD trading continued to operate smoothly and in an orderly manner during the review period. As neither the strong nor weak conversion guarantees were triggered during this period, the total reserves remained unchanged at approximately HKD 54 billion (Figure 4.2). Figure 4.1: HKD Exchange Rate; Figure 4.2: Total Reserves and Exchange Fund Bills and Notes. The nominal effective exchange rate index of the HKD broadly followed movements in the US dollar and edged up slightly during the review period (Figure 4.3). Given the small inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners, which had limited impact on the real effective exchange rate index, the trend of the real effective exchange rate index broadly mirrored that of the nominal effective exchange rate index. Figure 4.3: Nominal and Real Effective Exchange Rates. When measuring capital flows in Hong Kong, it is essential to distinguish between two distinct yet interrelated concepts: (1) HKD capital flows; and (2) cross-border capital flows. HKD capital flows focus on the currency dimension of capital movements, aiding the assessment of monetary stability, particularly under the linked exchange rate system. In contrast, cross-border capital flows emphasize the geographical movement of funds through Hong Kong's banking system, which helps assess the overall stability of Hong Kong's financial system. These two concepts require different monitoring indicators. When monitoring HKD capital flows, attention should be paid to the HKD exchange rate and total reserves. If the public or investors substantially convert their HKD assets into foreign currency assets, demand for the HKD would naturally decline, leading to a weaker HKD exchange rate. Under the linked exchange rate system, if the HKD exchange rate weakens to the weak conversion guarantee rate of HKD 7.85 per US dollar, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) stands ready to purchase HKD upon request from banks, thereby reducing total reserves. Since April 2019, total reserves have remained broadly unchanged, and the HKD exchange rate has been at the strong end of the exchange rate band in recent months; thus, no significant outflow of capital from the HKD was observed during the review period. When monitoring cross-border capital flows, the total amount of bank deposits in Hong Kong serves as a useful indicator. Significant capital outflows from Hong Kong's banking system would inevitably lead to a decline in bank deposits. During the review period, total deposits grew at a moderate pace, indicating no significant cross-border capital outflows. The continued smooth and orderly operation of Hong Kong's foreign exchange and currency markets suggests that the impact of the coronavirus outbreak on Hong Kong's monetary environment remains limited. However, risks arising from the coronavirus outbreak require close monitoring. With substantial foreign exchange reserves and a robust banking system, the HKMA possesses the capability, resources, and determination to manage capital outflows and maintain Hong Kong's monetary and financial stability. Despite an uncertain external environment and a slowing local economy, Hong Kong's monetary environment remained relatively loose during the review period. The HKD monetary base remained substantial, rising by 4.0% from the end of June to HKD 1,689.4 billion at the end of January 2020 (Figure 4.4). As no conversion guarantees were triggered during this period, total reserves remained broadly unchanged at approximately HKD 54 billion. Other components of the monetary base, including outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes, Certificates of Indebtedness, and currency notes and coins issued by the government, rose steadily. Figure 4.4: Components of the Monetary Base. During the review period, broad measures of HKD money supply remained broadly stable. HKD broad money supply (HKD M3) grew by 3.5% in the first half of 2019, followed by a slight increase of 0.2% over the seven months from the end of June 2019. Corresponding asset analysis indicates that the growth in HKD M3 since the end of June mainly reflected an increase in banks' net foreign currency assets and a rise in the monetary base (driven by increases in Certificates of Indebtedness and currency notes and coins issued by the government) (Figure 4.5). Over the seven months since the end of June, HKD deposits (the main component of HKD M3) remained broadly unchanged (Figure 4.6). Among HKD deposits, time deposits continued to grow moderately, partly reflecting higher HKD deposit interest rates. Figure 4.5: Changes in HKD M3 and Corresponding Assets. Over the seven months since the end of June 2019, foreign currency deposits grew moderately by 2.3% (Figure 4.6), primarily driven by US dollar deposits, which increased by 3.5% during this period. Other foreign currency deposits declined by 1.0% over the same period, with Renminbi (RMB) deposits, when valued in HKD, recording a slight decline. Overall, total deposits of authorized institutions grew steadily by 1.2% since the end of June. Supported by the increase in total deposits, Hong Kong's total broad money supply also rose at a relatively stable pace, with total money supply M2 and M3 increasing by 1.6% and 1.5% respectively since the end of June (Figure 4.7). Monthly monetary statistics may be subject to fluctuations due to various short-term factors (such as seasonal and IPO-related funding demands, as well as business and investment-related activities); therefore, statistics should be interpreted with caution. Figure 4.6: Authorized Institutions' Deposits by Currency; Figure 4.7: Total Broad Money Supply (M2). Although the monetary environment remained relatively loose, short-term HKD Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate (HIBOR) rates exhibited volatility, reflecting seasonal liquidity demands and increased capital market activities since the fourth quarter of 2019, particularly heightened IPO activity in the Hong Kong stock market. The overnight HKD HIBOR experienced notable fluctuations in late October and mid-November (Figure 4.8). During the review period, other short-term HKD HIBOR rates generally rose. Large IPO subscriptions exerted significant pressure on overnight rates; Feature Box 4 provides empirical analysis showing that market anticipation of future IPO activity can also affect the three-month HKD HIBOR. This occurs when market participants estimate future subscription deadlines for large IPOs and arrange medium-term funding in advance. Figure 4.8: HKD and USD Interbank Offered Rates. Regarding the HKD yield curve, it shifted downward following the US dollar yield curve. Compared with the end of June 2019, the yield on 10-year Hong Kong government bonds fell by 60 basis points to 1.04% on 28 February 2020 (Figure 4.9). Meanwhile, the yield on 3-year Hong Kong government bonds declined by 50 basis points over the same period to 1.00%. Figure 4.9: Government Bond Yields, Composite Rate, and Average Rate on New Mortgage Loans. At the retail level, the composite rate, reflecting the average cost of HKD funds for retail banks, gradually rose from 0.94% at the end of July 2019 to 1.01% at the end of January 2020. This increase mainly reflected banks' continued adjustment of preferential deposit rates to attract deposits, leading to a rise in the HKD-weighted deposit rate. At the end of October 2019, following the Federal Reserve's reduction in the target range for the federal funds rate, several retail banks lowered their prime lending rates by 12.5 basis points. Consequently, retail banks' prime lending rates currently range between 5.00% and 5.50%. Regarding mortgage loans, for mortgages pegged to HIBOR, major banks raised the interest rate caps determined by their prime lending rates, causing the average rate on new mortgages to rise to around 2.63% in October. The market's prime lending rate was lowered since November, leading to a slight decline in the average mortgage rate to 2.53% in January 2020. In response to evolving risks posed by the coronavirus outbreak to US economic activity and to support the Federal Reserve in achieving its policy objectives, the Fed cut the target range for the federal funds rate by a cumulative 150 basis points to 0–0.25% on 3 March and 15 March (US time). Although HKD HIBOR rates tend to follow US dollar interest rates in the long run, short-term HKD HIBOR rates may be influenced by local factors affecting HKD demand, such as IPO activity in Hong Kong. The banking system's total reserves have declined since April 2018, potentially increasing the sensitivity of HKD HIBOR to changes in HKD funding supply and demand. However, this does not imply that the current total reserves level of HKD 54 billion is insufficient to meet interbank payment settlement needs. In fact, Hong Kong's interbank market has continued to operate in an orderly manner. In the event of short-term liquidity shortages, banks can utilize liquidity facilities provided by the HKMA. Given the potential escalation of the US-China trade conflict, offshore and onshore RMB exchange rates weakened significantly in late August and September 2019, with the offshore RMB against the US dollar falling to a ten-year low of 7.19 on 2 September (Figure 4.10). In October, amid market expectations of resumed US-China trade negotiations, the RMB depreciation trend reversed; both offshore and onshore RMB strengthened in the fourth quarter and briefly breached the 6.9 level in mid-January 2020 following the signing of the first phase US-China trade agreement. However, since the end of January, both offshore and onshore RMB have again faced downward pressure due to the coronavirus outbreak. The offshore RMB traded at a discount to the onshore RMB for most of May to August, largely at a premium in the latter part of 2019, and saw a brief widening of the discount at the end of January 2020; however, the spread between the two remained moderate by historical standards. Figure 4.10: Onshore and Offshore RMB Exchange Rates. Despite fluctuations in the RMB exchange rate, liquidity conditions in the offshore RMB interbank market remained broadly stable. During the review period, the three-month offshore RMB HIBOR continued to hover between 3% and 4% (Figure 4.11). The overnight offshore RMB HIBOR experienced brief volatility in late August and late November due to the MSCI A-share adjustment, and again at the end of January 2020 approaching the Lunar New Year holiday.

Due to increasing uncertainties in the global and local economic environments, profits of Hong Kong's retail banks recorded a slight decline in the second half of 2019. Nevertheless, the capital and liquidity positions of the Hong Kong banking sector remain strong and稳健 when measured against international standards. Asset quality remains at a healthy level by historical standards. Although the growth rate of total loans slowed in the second half of last year, it still outpaced deposit growth during the review period. Correspondingly, both the average loan-to-deposit ratio across all currencies and the HKD loan-to-deposit ratio for all authorized institutions rose. However, given that the aggregate balances in the banking system remained stable and deposits were broadly steady, the liquidity position of the banking sector remained robust. Looking ahead, the Hong Kong banking sector will continue to face multiple downside risks, including uncertainties stemming from the spread of the coronavirus, future US-China trade relations, geopolitical tensions, and local social events. In light of the continued rise in corporate leverage levels and personal debt burdens, banks should prudently assess the impact on the asset quality of their loan portfolios under scenarios where these risk factors may intensify. In the second half of 2019, the overall pre-tax operating profit of retail banks was HK$59 billion, representing a slight decline of 1.5% compared to the same period in 2018. Correspondingly, the return on assets dipped slightly to 1.13% in the second half of 2019, lower than 1.23% in the same period of 2018 (Figure 5.1). Although the net interest margin of retail banks narrowed slightly from 1.67% in the second half of 2018 to 1.63% in the same period of 2019 (Figure 5.2), net interest income of retail banks continued to record moderate growth during the review period. However, both loan impairment provisions and operating expenses of retail banks increased, leading to a slight decline in profits. Figure 5.1: Retail Bank Profits; Figure 5.2: Net Interest Margin of Retail Banks. Despite three downward adjustments of 25 basis points each to the US Federal Funds target rate in the second half of 2019, no significant downward pressure has emerged so far in the HKD wholesale funding market. On the contrary, influenced by several local factors—including seasonal funding demands, increased liquidity needs due to large initial public offerings, and tighter interbank market liquidity conditions—short-term HKD interbank offered rates have been on an upward trend since the fourth quarter of 2019. Meanwhile, during the review period, longer-term HKD interbank offered rates remained broadly stable, with the three-month HKD HIBOR at the end of 2019 standing at 2.43%, close to the level six months prior (blue line in Figure 5.3). At the retail level, given that HKD savings deposit rates remain near zero, retail banks had limited room to follow the US policy rate cuts. On the other hand, due to tightening HKD liquidity in the banking system during the review period, banks continued to compete for long-term stable deposit funds. Reflecting an increase in the weighted funding cost of HKD deposits, the composite rate (an indicator measuring the average HKD funding cost of retail banks) gradually rose from 0.95% six months ago to 1.09% by the end of 2019, though it remained at a relatively low level by historical standards (green line in Figure 5.3). Figure 5.3: Interest Rates. From a more comprehensive perspective, given that the decline in USD funding costs for licensed banks in Hong Kong offset the slight increase in their HKD funding costs, the average overall HKD and USD funding costs for licensed banks in Hong Kong dipped by 14 basis points in the second half of 2019 (Figure 5.4). During the review period, banks' net interest income benefited from the slight decline in their overall funding costs and the relatively high level of HKD interbank offered rates, thereby supporting banking sector profits during the same period. Figure 5.4: HKD and USD Funding Costs and Maturities for Licensed Banks. Note 1: Since June 2019, all licensed banks required to comply with the new on-balance sheet interest rate risk framework in Hong Kong will submit returns under the new framework, while exempted licensed banks will continue to submit returns under the existing interest rate risk framework. Overall funding costs and maturities have been calculated as weighted averages based on the relevant figures for these two categories of licensed banks. Therefore, figures from June 2019 onwards cannot be directly compared with those of previous months. Looking ahead, multiple external and local downside risk factors will continue to cast a shadow over banks' profit prospects. Relevant factors include uncertainties arising from the spread of the coronavirus, the trajectory of future US-China trade relations, and intensifying geopolitical tensions. The intensification of these risk factors may undermine already weak global economic growth momentum and reduce demand for bank credit. Given that major central banks have widely adopted accommodative monetary policies, the global low-interest-rate environment may persist, which could exert pressure on banks' future net interest margins. At the local level, local social events since mid-2019 have continued to dampen business investment and market confidence. Against the backdrop of an already weak economic environment, if the situation persists or even intensifies in the future, it may lead to a deterioration in credit demand prospects and bank asset quality. In terms of overall market development, following the issuance of eight virtual bank licenses by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, the Hong Kong banking sector has begun to launch virtual banking services. As these new market participants may seek to increase their market share by offering more convenient products and more attractive deposit rates to attract new customers, this could exert upward pressure on the funding costs of existing banks. Although the short-term impact may remain moderate due to the currently limited business scale of virtual banks, their long-term impact may depend on whether existing banks accelerate the adoption of financial technology to maintain competitiveness. The results of Feature 5 show that the extent to which Hong Kong banks adopt financial technology is statistically correlated with improvements in cost efficiency and enhancements in profit levels. The capital base of the Hong Kong banking sector remains robust and far exceeds minimum international standards. As of the end of 2019, the consolidated total capital ratio of locally registered authorized institutions further rose to 20.7% (Figure 5.5). The Tier 1 capital ratio also increased to 18.5%, of which 16.5% was Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital. Figure 5.5: Capital Base of Locally Registered Authorized Institutions. In addition to risk-weighted capital adequacy ratios, the non-risk-weighted leverage ratio requirement under Basel III is designed to limit excessive leverage in the banking system. The leverage ratio of locally registered authorized institutions remained at a robust level of 8.2% at the end of 2019, well above the statutory minimum of 3% (Figure 5.6). Figure 5.6: Leverage Ratio of Locally Registered Authorized Institutions. Measured by the "Liquidity Coverage Ratio" requirement under Basel III, the liquidity position of the banking sector remained robust during the review period. The average Liquidity Coverage Ratio for Category 1 institutions rose from 152.8% in the second quarter of 2019 to 159.9% in the fourth quarter of 2019 (Figure 5.7), far exceeding the statutory minimum requirement of 100%. The average Liquidity Maintenance Ratio for Category 2 institutions also rose moderately from 54.6% in the second quarter of 2019 to around 56.3% in the fourth quarter of 2019, also well above the statutory minimum requirement of 25%. Figure 5.7: Liquidity Coverage Ratio and Net Stable Funding Ratio. The Net Stable Funding Ratio, as one of the liquidity standards under Basel III, indicates the stability of authorized institutions' funding positions. The average Net Stable Funding Ratio for Category 1 institutions remained at a high level of 131.7% in the fourth quarter of 2019 (Figure 5.8), far exceeding the statutory minimum requirement of 100%. The average Core Funding Ratio for Category 2A institutions remained at a high level of 134.5%, also exceeding the statutory minimum requirement of 75% applicable in 2019. The ample liquidity and robust funding positions of authorized institutions indicate that the Hong Kong banking sector is capable of withstanding various liquidity shocks. Figure 5.8: Net Stable Funding Ratio. Customer deposits remain the primary source of funding for authorized institutions, reflecting a stable funding structure in the banking system. At the end of 2019, the proportion of customer deposits in the total liabilities of all authorized institutions remained basically unchanged, dipping slightly from 56.4% six months prior to 56.3% (Figure 5.9). Figure 5.9: Liability Structure of All Authorized Institutions. The average HKD loan-to-deposit ratio for all authorized institutions rose from 89.3% at the end of June 2019 to 90.3% at the end of 2019 (Figure 5.10), as HKD loans and advances remained broadly stable while deposits declined slightly during the review period. Meanwhile, due to foreign currency loan growth outpacing deposit growth, the average foreign currency loan-to-deposit ratio also rose from 58.9% to 60.4% during the same period. Overall, the average loan-to-deposit ratio across all currencies for all authorized institutions rose from 74.5% at the end of June 2019 to 75.4% by the end of the year. Given that aggregate balances in the banking system have remained stable since April 2019 and deposits have been broadly steady, there were no obvious signs of significant capital outflows from HKD or the Hong Kong banking system during the review period. Figure 5.10: Average Loan-to-Deposit Ratio of All Authorized Institutions. The interest rate risk exposure of locally registered licensed banks remained at a relatively low level in the fourth quarter of 2019. We estimate that under a shock scenario of a 200 basis point increase in HKD and USD interest rates, the potential decline in the economic value of interest rate positions for locally registered licensed banks would amount to approximately 1.56% of their total capital base at the end of 2019 (Figure 5.11). Figure 5.11: Impact of HKD and USD Interest Rate Shocks on Locally Registered Licensed Banks. Against the backdrop of strained US-China trade relations, slowing global economic growth, and ongoing local social events, after a moderate rebound in the first half of 2019, bank credit growth slowed in the second half. On a half-year basis, loan growth (measured by the change in the total amount of loans and advances of all authorized institutions) grew moderately by 4.2% in the first half of 2019, then slowed to 2.4% in the second half (Figure 5.12). The slowdown in loan growth was due to the decelerating growth trends in both local loans (including loans used within Hong Kong and trade finance) and loans used outside Hong Kong during the review period. Local loans and loans used outside Hong Kong grew by 2.5% and 2.2% respectively in the second half of 2019, lower than the increases of 4.5% and 3.5% in the first half. Nevertheless, the total loan growth for the full year of 2019 still rose moderately to 6.7%, higher than 4.4% for the full year of 2018.

The rollout of vaccines against the novel coronavirus has brought hope for economic reopening and bolstered global growth prospects. Coupled with continued fiscal and monetary easing policies, financial markets have repeatedly reached new highs. However, the global outlook remains clouded by uncertainties, with recovery expected to be uneven across economies. In the medium term, the disconnect between financial markets and the real economy, elevated debt levels, and the lasting scars left by the pandemic on the economy will pose challenges for policymakers. Hong Kong's foreign exchange and money markets continued to function smoothly and in an orderly manner. The Hong Kong dollar traded close to the strong-side conversion rate, primarily driven by equity-related demand. During the review period, total deposits increased, with no signs of significant capital outflows from Hong Kong's banking system. Partially reflecting weak economic activity and reduced credit demand due to the recurrent pandemic, total bank loans declined slightly in the second half of the year, though they still recorded a modest increase on a full-year 2020 basis. Meanwhile, the residential property market remained broadly stable. Looking ahead, uncertainties regarding the pace of economic recovery and ongoing geopolitical risks will continue to pose challenges for Hong Kong's banking sector. In particular, the pandemic may weaken the repayment capacity of businesses and households, and the banking sector should remain vigilant regarding the impact of these downside risk factors on asset quality. Global economic growth rebounded in the third quarter of 2020 as economies worldwide reopened, but from the fourth quarter onward, rising numbers of novel coronavirus infections led to a renewed slowdown in global growth. Nevertheless, with breakthroughs in vaccine development by the end of 2020, market expectations were that the pandemic would eventually come to an end, facilitating a return to normalcy and accelerating global economic growth. Coupled with continued fiscal and monetary easing policies, global financial markets reached new highs in early 2021, although signs of a disconnect from the real economy began to emerge. Against this backdrop, uncertainties will continue to cloud the global economic outlook. Whether vaccines can be widely distributed remains to be seen. Meanwhile, supply bottlenecks and earlier aggressive easing policies could lead to inflation higher than expected, prompting central banks to reduce monetary easing ahead of schedule and ending market expectations of "lower-for-longer" interest rates. In the long run, policymakers need to assess the costs and benefits of extending relief measures and address numerous economic legacy issues triggered by the pandemic, including elevated global debt levels and lasting economic scarring. In East Asia, domestic GDP growth improved in the second half of 2020, supported by a rebound in export demand. With increased risk appetite, inflows of securities investment funds into the region recovered, and carry-trade activities re-emerged. Despite these positive developments, the East Asian region still faces persistent uncertainties stemming from the pandemic. First, in the global competition for vaccine procurement, less developed economies in the region may lag behind advanced economies in achieving herd immunity, hindering the recovery of their tourism and service sectors. Second, uncertainties regarding vaccine supply, coverage, or efficacy, coupled with deteriorating fiscal positions of regional governments, could dampen market sentiment and trigger capital flow reversals. As for mainland China, with consumption activities gradually returning to normal, the pace of economic recovery accelerated in the second half of 2020. For the full year of 2020, mainland China's economy grew by 2.3%, making it the only major economy to record positive growth. Looking ahead, the economic outlook will still largely depend on the evolution of the pandemic and changes in US-China tensions. The latest consensus forecast indicates that mainland China's economy will grow by 8.4% in 2021. The renminbi depreciated for several months in early 2020 but strengthened for the remainder of the year, driven by an accelerating economic recovery, a weakening US dollar, and strong capital inflows into the mainland bond market. Detailed studies show that during the novel coronavirus outbreak, fundamental factors rather than market sentiment played a more important role in driving renminbi exchange rate fluctuations (see Feature 1 for details). Hong Kong's economy improved in the second half of 2020, but real GDP remained far below pre-pandemic levels. With a slight increase in local demand and further expansion of goods exports, seasonally adjusted real GDP began to recover in the third quarter, ending a streak of five consecutive quarters of contraction. The year-on-year contraction in real GDP also narrowed significantly from 9% in the first half of 2020 to about 3% in the second half. However, for the full year of 2020, real GDP fell by 6.1%, the largest decline on record and the first time in history that the economy contracted for two consecutive years, following a 1.2% contraction in 2019. Latest data on GDP by sector shows that consumption- and tourism-related sectors contracted more severely than the overall economy under the pandemic. To address the ongoing pandemic, the Government launched two additional rounds (the third and fourth rounds) of the Anti-Epidemic Fund in the second half of 2020 to support affected industries and residents and enhance Hong Kong's pandemic response capabilities. The Government also announced additional counter-cyclical measures in the recent 2021-22 Financial Budget to boost the economy, including the issuance of one-off HK$5,000 electronic vouchers and 100% guaranteed personal special loans for unemployed individuals. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA), together with the "Banking SME Loan Coordination Mechanism," announced in March 2021 the extension of the "Interest-only, Principal-deferred" pre-approved scheme to October of the same year, and also extended the repayment period for trade finance loans under the scheme. These extension measures are expected to help alleviate liquidity difficulties faced by some corporate clients. Novel coronavirus vaccines are expected to facilitate a return to normal economic activity, with the local economy projected to resume positive growth in 2021 (on a full-year basis). However, the strength and pace of economic recovery will be influenced by numerous uncertainties, including the evolution of the pandemic and the progress and effectiveness of vaccine rollout. Given that widespread vaccination will take time, the local economy will still face significant challenges in the early part of 2021. Regarding external factors, mainland China's economy is expected to strengthen further, providing support for Hong Kong's exports of goods and services, while the recovery pace of other major economies will depend on the effectiveness of their large-scale vaccination programs. The Government forecasts real GDP growth for 2021 to be between 3.5% and 5.5%, while the average growth forecast from international institutions and private analysts stands at 4.4%. Labor market conditions deteriorated further in the second half of 2020 and early 2021. The unemployment rate continued to rise, reaching a 17-year high of 7.2% in February 2021, while the underemployment rate also rose to 4.0%, a post-SARS high. To address the worsening labor market conditions, the Government launched the "Preserve Jobs" scheme under the second round of the Anti-Epidemic Fund, providing time-limited wage subsidies (from June to November 2020) to employers to help them retain staff. After the "Preserve Jobs" scheme concluded, the Government introduced other targeted measures (such as one-off subsidies) under the third and fourth rounds of the Anti-Epidemic Fund to further support industries severely hit by the pandemic. In the short term, due to weak economic conditions, the labor market is expected to remain under pressure. Feature 2 explores the potential impact of the rise and fall of the inbound tourism industry on the local labor market. Local inflationary pressure continued to ease over the eight-month period from mid-2020 to February 2021. The core consumer price inflation rate fell significantly year-on-year to 0.3% and 0.2% in the third and fourth quarters of 2020, respectively, and further declined to -0.5% and -0.1% in January and February 2021, respectively. The core inflation rate calculated on a three-month annualized basis, which reflects inflationary momentum, has remained at a low level despite slight fluctuations in recent months. Given that global and local economic conditions remain challenging, Hong Kong's inflationary pressure is likely to remain mild in the short term, particularly as local inflation will continue to be contained by the earlier slowdown in growth of newly signed private residential rents. Market consensus forecasts an overall inflation rate of 1.4% for 2021, a moderate level, while the Government forecasts core and overall inflation rates for 2021 at 1.0% and 1.6%, respectively. The Hong Kong dollar traded close to the strong-side conversion rate, primarily driven by equity-related capital demand, including from robust initial public offering (IPO) activities and southbound capital inflows via the Stock Connect programs (Shanghai-HK and Shenzhen-HK). IPO activities remained active in the first two months of 2021, keeping the Hong Kong dollar persistently strong. During the review period, the strong-side conversion rate was triggered 47 times in September and October 2020, with capital inflows totaling HK$263.3 billion. The strong-side conversion rate was triggered 85 times in total throughout 2020, with cumulative inflows of HK$383.5 billion. Overall, Hong Kong dollar transactions continued to function smoothly and in an orderly manner. Analyzed from a geographic perspective, total deposits increased during the review period, indicating no signs of significant capital outflows from Hong Kong's banking system. Although uncertainties related to the pandemic's evolution, the pace of economic recovery, and ongoing US-China tensions may exacerbate capital flow volatility, Hong Kong possesses ample foreign exchange reserves and a robust banking system, enabling it to withstand such volatility. With the triggering of the strong-side conversion rate increasing the total reserve balance, Hong Kong dollar interbank offered rates generally remained at very low levels. The composite interest rate, reflecting the average cost of Hong Kong dollar funds for retail banking, fell further from 0.71% at the end of June 2020 to 0.23% by the end of February 2021. Due to the lower cost of funds, the average mortgage interest rate for new mortgages also declined from 2.02% in June to 1.56% in January. On the other hand, the prime lending rates of major retail banks remained unchanged during the review period, ranging between 5.00% and 5.50%. As the onshore renminbi (CNY) exchange rate strengthened, the offshore renminbi (CNH) appreciated against the US dollar since late May 2020. For most of the review period, the offshore renminbi traded at a premium to the onshore renminbi, with an average premium of about 100 basis points in the fourth quarter, which remains moderate by historical standards. Hong Kong's offshore renminbi liquidity pool continued to expand in the second half of 2020. As of the end of January 2021, the balance of renminbi customer deposits and certificates of deposit increased to RMB 826.3 billion. Regarding other renminbi-related businesses, renminbi bank loans in Hong Kong decreased, while renminbi trade settlements grew, and the daily average transaction volume of the renminbi Real-Time Gross Settlement system remained at a high of RMB 1.1915 trillion throughout 2020. Hong Kong possesses efficient financial infrastructure, offering investors numerous cross-border capital flow channels connecting to the mainland. With the continued opening of the mainland's capital account, increasing demand from international investors for renminbi assets, and the deepening of regional economic and financial cooperation under the "Belt and Road" initiative and the "Greater Bay Area" strategy, Hong Kong's offshore renminbi business is expected to benefit. Supported by rising global stock markets and active purchases of Hong Kong stocks by mainland investors via the Stock Connect programs, Hong Kong's stock market rebounded after a significant adjustment at the beginning of the review period. The rise in global stock markets was driven by unprecedented monetary easing measures taken by major economies; market optimism regarding positive progress in vaccine development, which could accelerate the recovery of economic activity; and a reduction in global geopolitical uncertainties. Against this backdrop, the Hang Seng Index recovered ground after a sharp decline in 2020, rising 15.1% during the review period and briefly breaking through the 31,000-point mark in mid-February 2021 to reach a 32-month high. Supported by stable issuance volumes, the Hong Kong dollar and offshore renminbi bond markets continued to expand in the second half of 2020. Following substantial net capital outflows in the first half of 2020, market confidence quickly recovered as governments worldwide launched unprecedented economic stimulus measures, leading to a rebound in bond fund inflows into the local market. Although bond yields experienced a moderate rebound during the same period, global bond yields, including those in Hong Kong, remained near historical lows.

As breakthroughs in vaccine development were achieved, market expectations rose that the novel coronavirus pandemic would eventually be brought to an end, enabling the global economy to accelerate its growth thereafter. Coupled with the expectation of a "lower for longer" global monetary policy stance, investors did not retreat despite the resurgence of the pandemic at the end of 2020, and financial markets reached new highs in early 2021. However, the fervent expectations in financial markets have become disconnected from a macroeconomic environment that remains fraught with challenges. Should the strength of the economic recovery fall short of expectations, or if policy support is withdrawn earlier than anticipated (for instance, due to inflation exceeding expectations), asset prices could experience volatility. Looking ahead, policymakers face the difficult task of determining when to withdraw policy support and addressing numerous lingering issues left by the pandemic, including elevated debt levels and long-term economic scarring. The continued uncertainty surrounding the pandemic continues to cast a shadow over the economic recovery in East Asia, while emerging market economies with slower development in the region may face greater challenges in vaccine procurement and distribution. Any delays in the progress of vaccination programs could reverse current optimism, leading to instability in capital flows and financial markets. Regarding mainland China, with consumer activities gradually returning to normal, the pace of economic recovery accelerated in the second half of 2020. Looking ahead, the economic growth outlook remains highly uncertain, largely dependent on the development of the pandemic and changes in China-US tensions. Consequently, the government announced its intention to maintain a supportive policy stance and emphasized the importance of controlling systemic risks. Benefiting from the purchasing power released by the economic reopening, most major economies recorded real GDP growth in the third quarter of 2020 that was better than expected. However, since the fourth quarter, the number of novel coronavirus infections has risen again, prompting governments worldwide to reimpose lockdowns and social distancing measures, thereby weakening the global growth momentum once more. By the end of 2020, more transmissible variants of the virus emerged and subsequently spread globally, exacerbating the situation. Nevertheless, with breakthroughs in vaccine development and the approval of multiple vaccines for use at the end of 2020, market expectations remain that the pandemic will eventually end, allowing the global economy to return to normal and accelerate growth. Another driver supporting the global economic recovery stems from continued policy stimulus measures, including the commitment by major central banks to a "lower for longer" monetary policy stance amid weak inflation, as well as ongoing fiscal easing measures in major advanced economies, particularly the fiscal stimulus packages passed by the US Congress in December 2020 and March 2021. Correspondingly, in January 2021, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) raised its forecast for global GDP growth in 2021 to 5.5%, which is 0.3 percentage points higher than its October 2020 forecast (Figure 2.1). Figure 2.1: IMF Forecasts for Real GDP Growth Made in January 2021 and October 2020. Against this backdrop, market optimism intensified, driving up stock prices in cyclical sectors that typically benefit from economic recovery, which in turn propelled global stock prices and valuations to new highs in early 2021 (Figure 2.2). Figure 2.2: 12-Month Forward Price-to-Earnings Ratios of Major Stock Indices. However, while financial markets performed strongly, the macroeconomic situation remains challenging; the disconnect between the two could lead to volatility in asset markets under multiple risks. First, the prospect of controlling the pandemic depends on the ability to widely distribute vaccines, which remains to be seen. As of mid-March 2021, the global vaccination rate remained low (Figure 2.3). Although global mechanisms (such as COVAX) facilitate a fairer distribution of vaccines, due to limited supply, the problem of low vaccination rates in lower-income emerging market economies is expected to be more severe. If pandemic control falls short of expectations, various regions may need to extend social distancing and other restrictive measures, thereby undermining the global recovery outlook. Figure 2.3: Proportion of Population in Selected Economies Who Have Received at Least One Dose of Vaccine (as of March 15, 2021). Second, the rebound in financial markets is built upon continued monetary and fiscal policy support, especially the "lower for longer" monetary policy. However, there is a risk that support measures could be withdrawn faster than expected. For example, driven by the combined effects of supply bottlenecks, strong currencies, liquidity growth, and active fiscal easing policies, inflation expectations in the US and Europe have already heated up (Figure 2.4). If future inflation proves stronger than expected, central banks may need to reduce the scale of monetary easing, and inflation data exceeding expectations could also lead to greater volatility in financial markets. Figure 2.4: 5-Year/5-Year Inflation-Linked Swap Rates in the US and Euro Area. Third, there is significant uncertainty regarding the future of China-US relations. The wave of "decoupling" between China and the US, particularly in the financial and technology sectors, has intensified since the outbreak of the pandemic. Given the increasingly hardline attitudes of both the Democratic and Republican parties in the US towards mainland China, this trend may not reverse under the Biden administration. An unexpected escalation in the China-US situation could trigger financial market turbulence in the future. Looking ahead, policymakers will need to face the difficult question of whether and when to withdraw pandemic-related support measures. While withdrawing these measures too early could harm the economic recovery and cause a "cliff effect," in the long run, the cost of these measures is high, including fiscal burdens and delays in the necessary reallocation of resources after the pandemic, such as allowing "zombie enterprises" with unviable business models to survive under continued government support. Furthermore, policymakers must also address the numerous issues left by the pandemic. First, due to declining corporate revenues and a surge in government spending, global debt levels rose significantly in 2020 (Figure 2.5). Although the problem posed by the rapid rise in debt may not be imminent given that global interest rates are currently at extremely low levels, continued debt accumulation in both the public and private sectors could raise concerns among markets regarding fiscal sustainability and financial stability. Figure 2.5: Global Debt as a Percentage of GDP. Another lingering issue involves the potential long-term economic losses or scarring caused by the pandemic. For example, high uncertainty may lead companies to reduce investment, while workers plagued by long-term unemployment may permanently exit the labor market, resulting in a significant waste of human resources. In East Asia, real GDP growth stabilized in the second half of the year after a sharp decline in the second quarter of 2020 (Figure 2.6). The momentum for economic recovery primarily came from a rebound in exports, with the strongest demand for electronics and technical equipment. Meanwhile, the service sector, which was hit hardest (such as tourism and consumer services requiring face-to-face contact with customers), continued to struggle. Figure 2.6: East Asia: Real GDP Growth in 2020. Despite uncertainties remaining in the economic recovery, securities investment funds have begun to flow back in. Since the second half of last year, improved market sentiment and higher yields compared to bonds in advanced economies have attracted more bond capital inflows to the region (Figure 2.7). As signs of economic recovery emerged and vaccine production plans were launched, equity capital inflows to East Asia also accelerated in the last quarter of 2020. Regional currencies also appreciated correspondingly due to securities capital inflows, causing the Bloomberg JPMorgan Asia Currency Index to rebound by approximately 10% from its low in March of last year. Figure 2.7: East Asia: Securities Investment Capital Flows. The East Asian region continues to face persistent uncertainties regarding the pandemic. First, although the rollout of vaccines has brought hope to the region's hard-hit service sector and economy, global competition for early-batch vaccines has driven up procurement costs, and vaccine distribution also poses challenges to the region's logistics and public health capabilities. Therefore, economies with slower development in the region may achieve herd immunity later than advanced economies, and uneven vaccination rates across different economies could prolong border closure periods and delay the recovery of tourism-related industries. Second, since investor optimism is largely driven by the vaccine rollout, if the progress or efficacy of vaccination falls far short of expectations, the current capital inflows and rebound in financial asset prices could come to an end. A sharp reduction in capital inflows could trigger another wave of market turbulence. With the novel coronavirus successfully brought under control and consumption gradually recovering, the mainland economy rebounded rapidly in the second half of 2020. At the same time, benefiting from strong demand for pandemic-related products (such as medical supplies and high-tech products), exports also maintained growth (Figure 2.8). Looking at 2020 as a whole, despite the unprecedented shock caused by the novel coronavirus pandemic, mainland China's GDP still recorded growth of 2.3%. Figure 2.8: Mainland China: Contribution of Various Demand Components to GDP Growth. Looking ahead, the latest consensus forecasts indicate that mainland China's economy will grow strongly by 8.4% in 2021, with private consumption expected to become the main driver of economic growth. However, whether the economy can continue to recover still depends to a certain extent on the development of the pandemic. Although industrial production activities in mainland China have normalized, the service sector continues to be partially disrupted as the pandemic resurged in several northern provinces. Regarding the external environment, although exports resumed growth in the second half of 2020, global demand remains uncertain as most developed economies experienced a new wave of the pandemic. Furthermore, the tense situation between China and the US may not ease in the short term; however, the previously signed Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP) and the concluded China-EU Comprehensive Agreement on Investment will help China integrate further with other economies, potentially partially offsetting the adverse impact of China-US decoupling on economic recovery. Considering that the economic outlook remains full of uncertainties, at the Central Economic Work Conference in December 2020, the government announced that the existing policy stance would not undergo significant changes in 2021 to support economic growth, while simultaneously emphasizing the importance of controlling systemic risks, such as maintaining the stability of macro leverage and the sustainability of local government debt. Additionally, the latest government work report set the growth target for 2021 at above 6%. In the long term, the "14th Five-Year Plan" identifies technological self-reliance and the dual circulation strategy as priority development directions, aiming to bring per capita GDP to the level of moderately developed countries by 2035. The impact of the novel coronavirus outbreak on the repayment capacity of bond-issuing enterprises appears to be limited, and the overall default rate in mainland China's bond market remained at a low level in the second half of 2020. However, due to a significant rise in defaults by state-owned enterprise bonds, the total amount of defaulted bonds increased in 2020 (Figure 2.9). Although the rise in state-owned enterprise defaults mainly reflects the central government's determination to break the "implicit guarantee" of state-owned enterprises to promote more reasonable market risk pricing, limited fiscal space in some local governments may also be a contributing factor, particularly in less developed regions. Figure 2.9: Mainland China: Onshore Bond Default Scale and Proportion. In the second half of 2020, financing costs for corporate issuers increased, particularly for some high-risk issuers. Although the continued economic recovery and gradual normalization of interest rates contributed to a certain extent to the rise in financing costs for lower-rated issuers, several corporate default events in the last quarter of 2020 caused credit spreads to widen significantly (Figure 2.10). Figure 2.10: Mainland China: 5-Year Corporate Bond Yield. Regarding the real estate market, property prices in mainland China continued to rise in the second half of 2020, especially in first-tier cities. In contrast, the pace of price increases in lower-tier cities was much slower (Figure 2.11). As for the issue of housing supply oversupply that plagued third-tier cities in previous years, it was basically under control in 2020, partly because third-tier cities recorded strong sales amidst high market sentiment. By the end of 2020, the inventory sales ratio in third-tier cities remained around 13 months, far below the peak of 31 months in early 2015.

Although real Gross Domestic Product (GDP) remains significantly below pre-pandemic levels, Hong Kong's economy improved in the second half of 2020, driven by a recovery in local demand and further expansion in goods exports. With expectations that vaccination against the novel coronavirus will restore economic activity to normal, the local economy is projected to return to growth in 2021 following the most severe contraction on record in 2020. However, the strength and pace of the economic recovery are subject to numerous uncertainties, including the evolution of the pandemic and the rollout and effectiveness of vaccines. Given that widespread vaccination will take time, the local economy will continue to face significant challenges in the early part of 2021. Consequently, the labour market is expected to remain under pressure in the short term, while local inflationary pressures are projected to remain mild. Hong Kong's economy improved in the second half of 2020 (Table 3.A), but economic activity remains far below pre-outbreak levels. The year-on-year decline in real GDP narrowed to 3.6% in the third quarter and further to 3.0% in the fourth quarter. However, for the full year of 2020, real GDP contracted by 6.1%, marking the largest decline on record and the first time in history that two consecutive years of contraction were recorded, following a 1.2% contraction in 2019. The latest GDP data by industry also indicate that the economic activities of the vast majority of industries registered year-on-year declines in recent quarters, with consumption- and tourism-related industries contracting more sharply than the overall economy. On a quarter-on-quarter basis, real GDP began to recover from the third quarter of 2020, ending a preceding five-quarter downward trend (Table 3.A and Figure 3.1). Local private consumption returned to positive growth in the third and fourth quarters; however, consumer confidence remained weak as authorities re-implemented social distancing measures amidst the third and fourth waves of the pandemic locally. With a brief improvement in business sentiment, overall investment expenditure also grew in the second half of the year. Benefiting in part from stronger export performance, particularly to mainland China, Hong Kong's goods trade expanded further (Figure 3.2). Given that the global tourism industry remains stagnant, services trade remains weak. Overall, net imports (trade deficit) weighed on GDP in the second half, partly reflecting that the recovery in goods exports was slower than that of imports. To address the ongoing pandemic, the Government launched two additional rounds (the third and fourth rounds) of the Anti-epidemic Fund between September and December 2020, totaling HK$30.4 billion, to assist industries and individuals affected by the pandemic and to enhance Hong Kong's pandemic response capacity. The Government also announced additional counter-cyclical measures in the recent 2021/22 Budget to boost the economy, including the issuance of one-off electronic vouchers of HK$5,000 and the provision of 100% guaranteed personal special loans for the unemployed. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA), together with the "Banking Sector SME Loan Coordination Mechanism," announced in March 2021 that the "Interest-Only Payment" scheme would be extended until October of the same year, and also extended the repayment period for trade financing loans under the scheme. These extension measures are expected to help alleviate liquidity difficulties faced by some corporate clients. With the novel coronavirus vaccine expected to restore economic activity to normal, Hong Kong's economy is projected to return to positive growth in 2021 (for the full year), although the strength and pace of the recovery remain subject to numerous uncertainties, including the evolution of the pandemic and the rollout and effectiveness of vaccines. Given that widespread vaccination will take time, the local economy will continue to face significant challenges in the early part of 2021. Regarding external factors, mainland China's economy is expected to strengthen further, providing support for Hong Kong's exports of goods and services, while the recovery pace of other major economies will depend on the effectiveness of their large-scale vaccination programs, thereby affecting Hong Kong's goods trade and inbound tourism. The Government forecasts real GDP growth for the full year of 2021 to be in the range of 3.5% to 5.5%, while the average growth forecast from international institutions and private sector analysts is 4.4%. Labour market conditions deteriorated further in the second half of 2020 and the early part of 2021. The seasonally adjusted unemployment rate rose further to 7.2% in February 2021, reaching a 17-year high (Figure 3.3). The underemployment rate also increased to 4.0%, a high level since the SARS outbreak. The total number of employed persons stabilized after falling to a low point (Figure 3.3), while Government figures indicate that the number of job vacancies continued to decline. The nominal average salary index for employed persons, reflecting labour income, slowed to 2.0% in the third quarter of 2020, the lowest in nearly 11 years. To address the worsening labour market conditions, the Government launched the "Retain Employment Support Scheme" under the second round of the Anti-epidemic Fund, providing time-limited (June to November 2020) wage subsidies to employers to help them retain staff. Following the conclusion of the "Retain Employment Support Scheme," the Government introduced other targeted measures (such as one-off allowances) under the third and fourth rounds of the Anti-epidemic Fund to further support industries severely impacted by the pandemic.
