As the novel coronavirus pandemic raged, the inbound tourism industry rapidly plunged into recession, raising market concerns about the potential scarring effects of this crisis on the future recovery of the labour market. To this end, this feature article empirically analyzes the impact of a thriving inbound tourism industry on the local labour market, thereby exploring the potential implications of the current tourism downturn. Since 2000, the inbound tourism industry has experienced significant fluctuations (Figure B2.1). Specifically, the number of visitor arrivals decreased during the SARS (Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome) outbreak in 2003. Following the launch of the Individual Visit Scheme (IVS) in July of that same year, visitor numbers began to surge. Under the original IVS, mainland residents could apply individually for one to two visits per year, with each stay not exceeding seven days. The IVS was expanded from April 2009 to allow eligible residents with Shenzhen household registration to apply for an "Individual Visit" visa permitting multiple visits per year. Since then, the number of visitors from mainland China has increased significantly. Driven by new cross-border infrastructure connecting Hong Kong and mainland China, visitor arrivals reached record highs between the end of 2018 and the beginning of 2019. Subsequent local social events halved visitor numbers in the second half of 2019, and under the novel coronavirus pandemic, the inbound tourism industry has been stagnant since the end of January 2020. Figure B2.1: Visitor Arrivals and Related Policies. We use the tourism boom brought about by the IVS as a case study to explore the impact of the inbound tourism industry on local employment and income. We consider the IVS launched in 2003 to be akin to a random economic shock, as it was nearly exogenous in timing and unforeseeable by Hong Kong residents. Our primary analytical data come from population data in the Hong Kong Population Censuses or By-censuses. Specifically, we use the 5% samples from the Population Censuses or By-censuses conducted in 1996, 2001, 2006, 2011, and 2016. Furthermore, we define tourism-related industries as catering, retail, hotel, and transport industries. First, we adopt a "difference-in-differences" framework as our analysis approach, comparing the differences in employment outcomes before and after the implementation of the IVS between young workers (aged 20–40) belonging to the "treatment group" and older workers (aged 41–65) belonging to the "comparison group." We classify the younger group as the "treatment group" because they are still in the early stages of their careers and can more flexibly make significant changes to their employment choices in response to the exogenous growth of the inbound tourism industry. Since the impact of the tourism boom brought about by the IVS on the labour market can vary over time, we also employ an "event study" approach to identify effects that change over time. Our empirical results show that, compared with the older group, young workers (especially females and those with only secondary education) were more likely to enter tourism-related industries after the implementation of the IVS. Among these, the impact of the IVS on the probability of young women entering tourism-related industries was particularly significant and persistent, remaining at a level close to 5 percentage points (relative to the average difference in entry probability with the older group) from 2006 onwards (Figure B2.2). We also used a similar method to compare incomes between workers in tourism-related industries (treatment group) and those in non-tourism-related industries (comparison group). Estimation results indicate that after the implementation of the IVS, income growth for workers in tourism-related industries was higher than that for employees in non-tourism-related industries. Furthermore, compared with similar employees in other industries, female workers and those with lower educational qualifications employed in tourism-related industries experienced higher and rising income increases (3 to 20 percentage points) (Figure B2.3). Figure B2.2: Impact of the IVS on Female Employment. Figure B2.3: Impact of the IVS on Incomes of Female and Low-Education Workers. The above results are generally consistent with international experience, revealing that the tourism industry is an important source of employment, especially for young people, women, and workers with lower educational qualifications. In the case of Hong Kong, our findings also align with previous analyses, indicating that strong growth in the inbound tourism industry increased demand for lower-skilled labour, thereby improving the resilience of the labour market for lower-skilled workers. As the inbound tourism industry has fallen from a boom to a trough, these labour groups may be more affected and warrant close monitoring.

The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate remained close to the strong-side conversion rate, which was triggered multiple times between September and October 2020. Strong demand for the Hong Kong dollar was primarily driven by equity-related funding needs, including robust initial public offering (IPO) activities and southbound capital inflows via the Stock Connect schemes (Shanghai-Hong Kong and Shenzhen-Hong Kong). As the total balance increased to over HK$450 billion, Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates (HIBOR) declined across the board. Although uncertainties related to the evolution of the novel coronavirus pandemic, the pace of economic recovery, and ongoing US-China tensions may exacerbate capital flow volatility, Hong Kong possesses adequate foreign exchange reserves and a sound banking system capable of withstanding such pressures. The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate remained near the strong-side conversion rate, mainly driven by equity-related funding needs, including robust IPO activities and southbound capital inflows via the Stock Connect schemes (Figure 4.1). Although some proceeds from certain IPOs were remitted overseas, the exchange rate traded within a narrow band of 7.7505 to 7.7544 in November and December, supported by improved sentiment in the local equity market and expectations of rising funding needs towards year-end. With IPO activity remaining active in the first two months of 2021 (Figure 4.2), the Hong Kong dollar closed at 7.7568 against the US dollar on 26 February 2021. Overall, trading in the Hong Kong dollar continued to be smooth and orderly. During the review period, repeated triggering of the strong-side conversion rate led to an increase in the total balance, reflecting substantial capital inflows into the Hong Kong dollar. Between September and October 2020, the strong-side conversion rate was triggered 47 times. Under the design of the linked exchange rate system, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) sold a total of HK$263.3 billion, raising the total balance from HK$193.1 billion at the end of August to HK$457.5 billion at the end of February (Figure 4.3). The strong-side conversion rate was triggered 85 times in 2020, with cumulative inflows of HK$383.5 billion. From a cross-border perspective, the increase in total deposits indicates no signs of significant capital outflows from the local banking system. Meanwhile, the latest balance of payments data show that non-resident direct investment continued to flow into Hong Kong in the fourth quarter of 2020, with no indication of abnormal capital movements. Figure 4.1: Hong Kong Dollar Exchange Rate Figure 4.2: Equity Capital Raised on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange Figure 4.3: Total Balance and Exchange Fund Bills and Notes During the review period, the Hong Kong dollar nominal effective exchange rate index generally declined in line with the weakening of the US dollar against major currencies (Figure 4.4). Given the small inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners, which had limited impact on the Hong Kong dollar real effective exchange rate index, the latter's trend broadly followed that of the nominal index. Figure 4.4: Nominal and Real Effective Exchange Rates Looking ahead, uncertainties related to the pandemic's evolution, the pace of economic recovery, and ongoing US-China tensions may exacerbate capital flow volatility. As an international financial centre, Hong Kong hosts various fundraising activities, such as IPOs, resulting in substantial capital inflows and outflows. On one hand, these activities attract international investors to transfer funds to Hong Kong. On the other, funds raised by listed companies may subsequently be transferred out of Hong Kong for business needs. With adequate foreign exchange reserves and a sound banking system, Hong Kong is well-positioned to absorb capital flow volatility without compromising financial stability. Amid continuous capital inflows into the Hong Kong dollar, the local monetary environment remained loose in the second half of 2020 and in recent months. Over the eight months since the end of June 2020, the Hong Kong dollar monetary base increased by 20.8% (Figure 4.5). By component, this increase reflected the rise in the total balance due to repeated triggering of the strong-side conversion rate. Meanwhile, other components, including Certificates of Indebtedness, currency notes and coins issued by the Government, and outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes, remained relatively stable. Figure 4.5: Composition of the Monetary Base During the review period, large-scale IPO activities led to an increase in Hong Kong dollar deposits derived from IPO subscription loans, causing a significant rise in Hong Kong dollar broad money (HKM3) and its deposit component between July and October 2020 and in January 2021 (Figure 4.6). As IPO activities concluded and customers repaid their subscription loans, Hong Kong dollar deposits and broad money returned to normal levels by the end of 2020. In January 2021, HKM3 surged again, primarily driven by large-scale IPO activities at the end of the month. Overall, over the seven months since the end of June, HKM3 grew by 21.7%; excluding the impact of late-January IPOs, HKM3 rose moderately by 9.1%. Based on corresponding assets, excluding IPO subscription loans, the growth in HKM3 was mainly attributable to the increase in the monetary base triggered by the strong-side conversion rate (Figure 4.7). As a major component of HKM3, Hong Kong dollar deposits rose by 22.9% over the same period; excluding the impact of late-January IPOs, they grew moderately by 9.1%. Although time deposits declined due to low interest rates, this was fully offset by rapid growth in current and savings deposits, partly driven by investment demand. Figure 4.6: Deposits of Authorized Institutions by Currency Figure 4.7: Changes in HKM3 and Corresponding Assets Overall foreign currency deposits grew steadily by 3.6% over the seven months since the end of June. US dollar deposits edged down by 0.3%, partly reflecting the weakness of the US dollar, while other foreign currency deposits surged by 15.5% over the same period, mainly reflecting an increase in renminbi deposits. Overall, due to short-term fluctuations in Hong Kong dollar deposits triggered by IPO activities, total deposits of authorized institutions rose significantly by 13.2% during the review period (Figure 4.6). It should be noted that monthly monetary statistics may be subject to volatility from various short-term factors (such as seasonal and IPO-related funding needs, as well as business and investment activities), and thus should be interpreted with caution. As the total balance increased, HIBOR remained at very low levels overall during the review period (Figure 4.8). Due to the recurring novel coronavirus pandemic leading to a prolonged economic downturn, coupled with the impact of a persistently low-interest-rate environment, Hong Kong's retail banks recorded a further decline in profits in the second half of 2020, accompanied by a slight deterioration in asset quality. Nevertheless, given their robust capital and liquidity positions, Hong Kong's banking sector remained resilient. During the review period, to continue supporting the overall economy through this difficult phase, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) decided to extend several relief measures. Looking ahead, while the rollout of vaccines may foster optimism that the global pandemic could be brought under control and economic activity resumed, the pace of economic recovery remains uncertain. The aforementioned uncertainties and ongoing geopolitical tensions are adverse to business activities and will continue to pose challenges to Hong Kong's banking sector. In particular, as the pandemic weakens the repayment capacity of enterprises and households, the banking sector should remain closely attentive to the impact of these related downside risk factors on asset quality. In the second half of 2020, the overall pre-tax operating profit of retail banks fell by 38.5% compared with the same period in 2019. Correspondingly, the return on assets (ROA) declined to 0.62% in the second half of 2020, from 1.13% in the same period of 2019 (Figure 5.1). The net interest margin (NIM) of retail banks narrowed from 1.63% in the second half of 2019 to 1.01% in the same period of 2020 (Figure 5.2), resulting in a decrease in net interest income that outweighed the slight growth in non-interest income, thereby leading to a decline in profits. For the full year of 2020, the overall pre-tax operating profit of retail banks fell by 29.4%, and the ROA decreased from 1.19% in 2019 to 0.77%. Figure 5.1: Profits of Retail Banks; Figure 5.2: Net Interest Margin of Retail Banks. Largely driven by substantial capital inflows fueled by stock market activity, liquidity in the Hong Kong dollar (HKD) became more ample. The Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate (HIBOR) softened further in the fourth quarter of 2020. Specifically, the three-month HIBOR fell by 43 basis points in the second half of the year to 0.35% by the end of 2020 (blue line in Figure 5.3). The trend of the composite interest rate, an indicator measuring the average HKD funding cost of retail banks, was broadly similar, declining significantly from 0.71% at the end of June 2020 to 0.28% by the end of 2020 (green line in Figure 5.3). The decline in the composite interest rate primarily reflected lower interbank funding costs and reductions in time deposit rates by some major retail banks. Figure 5.3: Interest Rates. From a broader perspective, the average overall HKD and US dollar (USD) funding costs of licensed banks in Hong Kong moderated by 53 basis points in the second half of 2020 (red line in Figure 5.4). Figure 5.4: HKD and USD Funding Costs and Tenors of Licensed Banks. Looking ahead, as the global low-interest-rate environment is likely to persist and continue to adversely affect banks' net interest margin performance, the profit outlook for the banking sector will remain challenging. Furthermore, although breakthroughs in vaccine development have bolstered market optimism regarding the global economic outlook, given the significant uncertainties surrounding vaccine distribution and efficacy, the trajectory of economic recovery remains extremely unclear. These risk factors will continue to affect the loan quality and profitability of the banking sector in the near term. The capital base of Hong Kong's banking sector remains robust and significantly exceeds minimum international standards. The consolidated total capital ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions stood at 20.7% at the end of December 2020, well above the international minimum requirement of 8% (Figure 5.5). The Tier 1 capital ratio during the period was 18.7%, of which 16.7% constituted Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital. Additionally, the leverage ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions remained at a robust level of 8.2% at the end of December 2020, exceeding the statutory minimum of 3% (Figure 5.6). Figure 5.5: Capital Adequacy of Locally Incorporated Authorized Institutions; Figure 5.6: Leverage Ratio of Locally Incorporated Authorized Institutions. Measured against the Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) requirement under Basel III, the liquidity position of the banking sector remained robust during the review period. The average LCR of Class 1 institutions was 155.1% in the fourth quarter of 2020 (Figure 5.7), far exceeding the statutory minimum requirement of 100%. During the same period, the average Liquidity Maintenance Ratio of Class 2 institutions was 57.9%, also well above the statutory minimum of 25%. Figure 5.7: Liquidity Coverage Ratio. The most recent figures under the Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR) requirement also indicate stable funding conditions for authorized institutions. The average NSFR of Class 1 institutions and the average Core Funding Ratio of Class 2A institutions remained at high levels of 138.6% and 139.5%, respectively, in the fourth quarter of 2020 (Figure 5.8), significantly exceeding their respective statutory minimum requirements of 100% and 75%. The ample liquidity and robust funding conditions of authorized institutions indicate that Hong Kong's banking sector is capable of withstanding liquidity shocks. Figure 5.8: Net Stable Funding Ratio. Customer deposits remain the primary source of funding for authorized institutions, reflecting a stable funding structure within the banking system. At the end of 2020, customer deposits accounted for approximately 56.1% of the total liabilities of all authorized institutions, similar to the level six months prior (Figure 5.9). Figure 5.9: Liability Structure of All Authorized Institutions. As the total deposits of all authorized institutions increased in the second half of 2020 while the total loans decreased during the same period, the average loan-to-deposit ratio (LDR) of all authorized institutions in all currencies fell from 76.0% at the end of June 2020 to 72.3% by the end of 2020 (Figure 5.10). The increase in total deposits largely reflected growth in both HKD and foreign currency deposits. Correspondingly, as of the end of 2020, the average HKD LDR and foreign currency LDR declined to 83.5% and 61.0%, respectively, from 86.4% and 65.5% six months earlier. Figure 5.10: Average Loan-to-Deposit Ratio of All Authorized Institutions. The interest rate risk exposure of locally incorporated licensed banks remained at a relatively low level in the fourth quarter of 2020. Assuming a shock of a 200 basis point rise in HKD and USD interest rates, the estimated potential decline in the economic value of interest rate positions of locally incorporated licensed banks is equivalent to 1.41% of their total capital base at the end of December 2020 (Figure 5.11). Figure 5.11: Impact of HKD and USD Interest Rate Shocks on Locally Incorporated Licensed Banks. Against the backdrop of recurring pandemic outbreaks and tightened social distancing measures leading to a prolonged economic downturn, the total loans and advances experienced a moderate decline in the second half of 2020. However, for the full year of 2020, the total credit of the banking sector still recorded positive growth, albeit at a significantly slowed pace from 6.7% in 2019 to 1.2%. On a half-year basis, the total loans and advances of all authorized institutions, after growing by 3.0% in the first half of 2020, decreased by 1.8% in the second half (Figure 5.12). The decline in total loans was due to decreases in both local loans (including loans used within Hong Kong and trade financing) and loans used outside Hong Kong. Specifically, the total amount of local loans dipped slightly by 0.9% in the second half, while loans used outside Hong Kong contracted by 3.9%, whereas both had grown by 2.6% and 4.2%, respectively, in the first six months. Figure 5.12: Loan Growth. By currency, HKD loans, after declining by 2.0% in the first half, remained broadly at a level similar to that of the end of June by the end of 2020. Foreign currency loans, after surging by 10.6% in the first half of 2020, decreased by 4.5% in the second half, partly reflecting a decline in demand for USD loans as global liquidity conditions improved. The banking sector's outlook for short-term credit demand became slightly more optimistic compared to six months ago. The HKMA's "Credit Conditions Outlook Survey" in December 2020 showed that the proportion of surveyed authorized institutions expecting loan demand to increase over the next three months rose to 37%, while the proportion expecting loan demand to decrease over the same period fell to 13% (Table 5.A). Due to the adverse impact of the pandemic on the repayment capacity of households and companies, loan quality deteriorated slightly but remained robust by historical and international standards. Moreover, the pace of deterioration in loan quality also slowed in the second half of 2020. The total specific provision loan ratio of all authorized institutions rose moderately from 0.79% six months prior to 0.9% by the end of 2020, while the ratio of overdue and restructured loans of all authorized institutions increased from 0.49% at the end of June 2020 to 0.57% by the end of 2020. For retail banks, the total specific provision loan ratio and the ratio of overdue and restructured loans rose to 0.82% and 0.48%, respectively (Figure 5.13).

Entering 2022, the global economy performed weakly, while inflationary pressures continued to intensify across regions, particularly in the United States. Looking ahead, the global economic outlook faces significant uncertainties, including the risk of large-scale outbreaks of the pandemic, and the possibility that monetary policy tightening may exceed expectations if US inflation proves more persistent and widespread than anticipated. Should the Federal Reserve implement substantial monetary tightening, leading to tighter global financial conditions, this would place pressure on the recovery of more vulnerable emerging market economies. Recently, the outbreak of military conflict between Russia and Ukraine could have significant impacts on the global economy through trade and financial channels, further complicating the global monetary policy outlook. During the review period, the Hong Kong dollar weakened, but trading remained smooth and orderly. Total deposits grew moderately during the review period, with no significant signs of capital outflows from Hong Kong's banking system. For the full year of 2021, the growth in total bank loans accelerated. On the other hand, the residential property market has softened since mid-2021. Looking ahead, the rapid spread of the Omicron variant may threaten the continued economic recovery, and combined with the possibility that the pace of US monetary policy normalization may be faster than expected, these risk factors will pose challenges to banks' credit risk management. Banks should remain vigilant and carefully assess the potential impact of these relevant risk factors on the asset quality of their loan portfolios. The global economy began to slow down from late 2021, with weakness persisting into 2022, due to increased global travel restrictions caused by the spread of the highly contagious Omicron variant, alongside persistent supply bottlenecks that continued to constrain production. Meanwhile, under conditions of supply-demand imbalances and labor shortages, global inflationary pressures continued to intensify and have spread to a wide range of goods and services in major advanced economies, particularly the United States. Recently, following the outbreak of military conflict between Russia and Ukraine, a sharp rise in commodity prices could further exacerbate the threat of global inflation, while heightened financial market volatility may lead to less-than-desirable tightening of global financial conditions, making the global monetary policy outlook even more complex. Looking ahead, there are significant uncertainties in the global economic outlook. In the short term, in the event of large-scale outbreaks of the pandemic, the reimposition of lockdown measures and a renewed deterioration of supply bottlenecks cannot be ruled out. In the United States, as the risk of inflation becoming more persistent and widespread than expected grows, the Federal Reserve has adopted a more hawkish stance, accelerating its timeline for reducing asset purchases and raising interest rates, and has begun discussing balance sheet reduction. If the Federal Reserve needs to substantially tighten monetary policy, global financial conditions may also tighten, leading to a deterioration in borrowers' debt-servicing capacity, and disorderly capital outflows could place pressure on the recovery of relatively vulnerable emerging market economies. Recently, the military conflict between Russia and Ukraine may pose a risk of continued rises in global commodity prices, exacerbating shortages in industrial supplies and increasing financial market volatility. Heightened market volatility could also trigger redemption pressures on open-ended funds, increasing their liquidity risks. Feature 1 will discuss whether swing pricing (a liquidity management tool for open-ended funds) can reduce the liquidity risks of these funds during periods of market stress, and will examine the potential limitations of this tool. Regarding Emerging Asia, the economy continued to recover in the second half of 2021, although the recovery momentum temporarily slowed in the third quarter as some Southeast Asian economies reimposed strict pandemic control measures, while the region's technology product exporting economies (South Korea and Singapore) continued to benefit from strong global demand for technology products. Although the market generally expects a broad recovery in Emerging Asia in 2022, the region's short-term economic outlook faces multiple headwinds. First, new variants of the virus remain a concern, especially for economies within the region with lower vaccination rates and scarce public health resources. Second, the Federal Reserve's acceleration of policy normalization could trigger capital outflows from the region and intensify currency depreciation pressures; for regional economies that still need to maintain loose monetary policy to support economic recovery, the trade-off between curbing capital outflow pressures and supporting economic activity will become more difficult. Third, a slowdown in major economies, coupled with a potential shift in demand from goods to services as the global economy gradually reopens, will weigh on trade growth prospects. Fourth, the rise in prices of various commodities triggered by the conflict between Russia and Ukraine will be transmitted to regional inflation while simultaneously weakening consumption. Coupled with increased global economic uncertainty, the decision-making process for monetary policy normalization by regional central banks will become more complex. Central banks in some economies with weaker growth momentum and higher sensitivity of inflation to energy prices will face particularly difficult trade-offs. In the long term, to rebuild a sustainable and robust growth model, investors need to place greater emphasis on environmental, social, and governance (ESG) factors in their investment considerations. Feature 2 examines the sensitivity of stock returns to changes in climate risk and how this sensitivity is influenced by corporate environmental performance. Economic growth in mainland China slowed in the second half of 2021, affected by a new wave of coronavirus outbreaks, power rationing measures, and tightening measures in the real estate market. Looking ahead, due to the continued slump in the real estate market and the outbreak of the Omicron variant, the mainland economy may continue to face downward pressure in the short term. Therefore, mainland authorities have prioritized stabilizing growth as the primary task for this year and have introduced a series of fiscal and monetary support measures. The total amount of onshore bond defaults and onshore bond defaults by state-owned enterprises both decreased in the second half of 2021; Feature 3 discusses whether the pricing of state-owned enterprise bonds has improved in recent years. The overall risk in the banking sector remains controllable, as mainland banks (especially those with systemic importance) have limited exposure to loans for developers, and maintain lower non-performing loan ratios and higher provision coverage ratios. Hong Kong's economy continued to recover in the second half of 2021, although the pace slowed compared to the first half. Seasonally adjusted real Gross Domestic Product (GDP) grew moderately, benefiting from goods exports and private consumption, which were supported by the continued global economic recovery, improved local labor market conditions, and the government's voucher scheme. On a year-on-year basis, economic growth was 5.1% in the second half of 2021, compared to 7.8% in the first half. For the full year of 2021, economic growth was 6.4%, marking the first full year of positive growth since 2019. Entering 2022, a new wave of local infections and the resulting tightened social distancing measures placed pressure on Hong Kong's economic activities. The government launched the fifth and sixth rounds of the Anti-epidemic Fund and introduced additional counter-cyclical measures under the "2022-23 Budget" to support the economy. To support cash flow, the "100% Guarantee Personal Special Loan" and various guarantee products under the "SME Financing Guarantee Scheme" will be optimized, with higher maximum loan amounts, extended application periods, and longer repayment terms. The HKMA, together with the banking industry, also extended the "Pre-approved Interest-Only" scheme until the end of October 2022. The scheme also provides borrowers with a one-year partial principal repayment option, which is also applicable to loans under the "SME Financing Guarantee Scheme." Hong Kong's economy is expected to continue recovering over the full year of 2022, but the growth pace will be slower than in 2021, partly reflecting slower global growth amid the ongoing pandemic and higher base effects. Specifically, Hong Kong's goods exports will continue to benefit from global economic expansion. Government promotion of various capital works and infrastructure projects will also provide support to the economy. The government forecasts real GDP growth for 2022 to be between 2.0% and 3.5%, while the average growth forecast from international organizations and private sector analysts is 1.6%. However, the strength and pace of the economic recovery are influenced by several uncertainties and risks discussed in previous sections, particularly the pandemic and the pace of US monetary policy normalization. As the economy recovered, the labor market improved further in the second half of 2021, with the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate falling to 3.9% by year-end. Total employment rebounded but remained below pre-pandemic levels. In early 2022, official data showed that labor market pressures resurfaced amid the new wave of local infections. Additionally, a decline in the number of online recruitment advertisements also reflected a reduction in new job vacancies. The new wave of local infections and tightened pandemic control measures will place some pressure on the local labor market in the short term, especially in industries involving face-to-face contact. In the longer term, labor market conditions will depend on the development of the local pandemic and the pace of local economic recovery. Local inflationary pressures have increased somewhat in recent months but remain moderate. However, weak rental growth and moderate local labor cost pressures should contain overall price pressures. Market consensus forecasts overall inflation for 2022 to reach 2.4%, while the government expects overall inflation for 2022 to be 2.1%, with core inflation at 2.0%. Stimulated by government monetary and fiscal policies, the global economic recovery and strong corporate earnings drove major global stock markets higher overall in the last quarter of 2021, leading the Morgan Stanley Capital International World Index to a historic high of 3,262 points on January 4, 2022. Due to the rapid global spread of virus variants (Delta and Omicron) combined with persistent production bottlenecks, the global economy slowed significantly in the latter half of 2021, with growth momentum remaining weak as we entered 2022. Global inflationary pressures continued to intensify and have spread to a wide range of goods and services in major advanced economies, particularly the United States. Rising inflation concerns prompted the Federal Reserve to shift its monetary policy stance to a more hawkish position, exacerbating the risk that premature tightening of global financial conditions could weigh on currently elevated asset valuations, which is also unfavorable for emerging markets where recovery remains broadly lagging. Recently, the conflict between Russia and Ukraine has driven up energy and other commodity prices, triggered volatility in global financial markets, and intensified some of the aforementioned risks. In Emerging Asia, despite the spread of the Delta variant within the region, the economy continued to recover in the second half of 2021, with major technology-product exporting economies in the region continuing to outperform other economies. Although the Omicron variant is not expected to severely impede the region's economic recovery at present, any uncertainty related to new variants will continue to cast a shadow over the region's economic outlook. Additionally, the normalization of Federal Reserve policy may trigger adjustments in regional asset prices, while slowing growth in major economies could drag down regional goods export growth. The conflict between Russia and Ukraine, on one hand, has led to rising commodity prices and increased inflation risks, and on the other, has weakened consumption and heightened global economic uncertainty, making the decision-making process for monetary policy normalization by regional central banks more complex. Economic growth in mainland China slowed in the second half of 2021, affected by a new wave of novel coronavirus outbreaks, power rationing, and tightening measures in the real estate market. Looking ahead, the mainland economy may continue to face downward pressure from cooling in the real estate market and outbreaks of the Omicron variant. In light of this, the government has set stabilizing growth as its top priority for the year, and macroeconomic policies will provide greater support. The global economic recovery slowed markedly in the fourth quarter of 2021, as the highly transmissible Omicron variant overlapped with the spread of the Delta variant, triggering a new wave of infections and leading to tightened restrictions on personnel mobility worldwide. Furthermore, supply chain issues (such as shipping bottlenecks and shortages of key production raw materials like semiconductors) continued to constrain production. Entering 2022, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) predicted in January that global GDP growth would slow from 5.9% in 2021 to 4.4% in 2022, reflecting the continued drag of the pandemic and supply constraints, reduced policy support in the US and other major advanced economies, and slowing growth momentum in mainland China offsetting the expected growth rebound in other parts of Asia (Figure 2.1). Figure 2.1 IMF Real GDP Growth Forecasts. Amid the slowdown in global economic growth, inflationary pressures also continued to rise during the review period. Core inflation (excluding food and energy prices) rose significantly in major advanced economies, especially in the United States, which implemented larger-scale policy stimulus since the pandemic. Amid supply bottlenecks, pent-up demand being released, and labor shortages, inflationary pressures have spread to a wide range of goods and services (Figure 2.2). Additionally, the recent military conflict between Russia and Ukraine has pushed up prices for various commodities, which may exacerbate already elevated global inflationary pressures. Figure 2.2 Core Consumer Price Index Inflation Rates for Selected Economies (1) The latest data for the US, UK, and Eurozone are for January 2022; the rest are for December 2021. (2) "Advanced Asian Economies" include Australia, New Zealand, Japan, South Korea, Hong Kong, and Singapore. (3) "Emerging Market Asian Economies" include mainland China, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, and Thailand. Looking ahead, the global economic outlook faces significant uncertainties with considerable downside risks, and will depend on the evolution of the pandemic and related supply chain disruptions, how geopolitical tensions impact global trade, inflation, and financial market sentiment, and the policy response of major central banks to inflation. Regarding the pandemic, most governments have so far adopted targeted measures in response to the recent surge in Omicron cases, focusing on restricting high-risk activities, encouraging remote work, and promoting vaccination. Compared with previous lockdown policies, these more relaxed measures should help reduce supply chain disruptions, and preliminary signs of improvement in supply chain disruptions have emerged since the end of 2021 (Figure 2.3). However, in the event of large-scale outbreaks, the reimposition of lockdown measures cannot be ruled out, which could subsequently lead to a worsening of supply bottlenecks. Figure 2.3 Purchasing Managers' Index – Supplier Deliveries Index. If the pandemic remains under control, supply bottlenecks are expected to gradually improve, providing some relief to goods inflation. However, several developments could make the current situation of elevated global inflation more persistent than expected, including the risk that the military conflict between Russia and Ukraine and sanctions on energy imports from Russia will push up commodity prices; the lagged reflection of rising production costs in final selling prices; the potential for earlier sharp rises in global residential property prices to drive future rent increases; upward risks to wage growth from labor market tightness; and rising inflation expectations. In particular, given that US inflation has recorded the largest increase in decades, the Federal Reserve shifted to a more hawkish policy stance at its December 2021 Federal Open Market Committee meeting, no longer characterizing high inflation as "transitory," and doubled the pace of asset purchase tapering from a monthly reduction of $150 billion to $300 billion, aiming to end the asset purchase program by March 2022 and begin discussing balance sheet reduction. In fact, recent market pricing suggests the Federal Reserve may raise interest rates multiple times in 2022. In contrast, given the closer trade and financial ties between the Eurozone and Russia and Ukraine, the European Central Bank may face more significant policy trade-offs. In this context, coupled with persistently high levels of global debt and asset valuations under long-term accommodative policies, if persistent inflationary pressures force the Federal Reserve to tighten policy faster than expected, it could pose risks of deteriorating borrower solvency and trigger financial market volatility. Recently, with the escalation of geopolitical tensions in Eastern Europe, risk aversion in financial markets has risen, and signs of a US dollar shortage have emerged, including a widening of cross-currency swap spreads. Under conditions of premature tightening of global financial conditions, emerging market economies with weaker fundamentals and still affected by the pandemic may be vulnerable to renewed growth slowdowns, currency depreciation, and capital outflow pressures. Increased market volatility may also trigger redemption pressures on open-ended funds, increasing their liquidity risks. Feature 1 will discuss whether swing pricing (a liquidity management tool for open-ended funds) can reduce the liquidity risks of these funds during market stress, and discuss the potential limitations of this tool. In Emerging Asia, economic recovery continued in the second half of 2021, but the spread of the Delta variant weakened growth momentum in the third quarter, particularly in some Southeast Asian economies (Figure 2.4). Meanwhile, as major technology product export hubs in the region, South Korea and Singapore continued to benefit from strong global demand for technology products, which further widened the imbalance in recovery across the region. Additionally, inflationary pressures in several Emerging Asian economies remain moderate. Figure 2.4 Manufacturing Purchasing Managers' Index. The market generally expects a broad recovery in Asian emerging markets in 2022, but the region's short-term economic outlook faces multiple headwinds: First, although the Omicron variant has spread within the region since the end of 2021, its economic impact remains milder than previous infection waves; however, some regional economies with lagging vaccination rates and relatively tight public health resources will continue to face threats from new variants. Second, the normalization of Federal Reserve policy may trigger capital outflows and create depreciation pressure on regional currencies. Regional economies that still need to maintain accommodative monetary policy to support economic recovery will face more difficult trade-offs between curbing capital outflow pressures and supporting economic activity. At the long end of the yield curve, due to the high historical correlation between the two (Figure 2.5), the risk of a sudden surge in US long-term yields will also spread to long-term bond yields in Emerging Asia, intensifying the risk of adjustments in regional asset markets. Figure 2.5 Correlation between Asian 10-Year Sovereign Bond Yields and Corresponding US Treasury Yields. Third, the outlook for regional commodity trade faces uncertainties from slowing growth in major economies and the possibility that demand may shift from goods to services as the global economy gradually reopens, factors that could weaken regional export growth. Figure 2.6 US: Imports from Emerging Asia and Real GDP. Fourth, although the trade and financial links between regional economies and Russia and Ukraine are relatively limited, the rise in commodity prices triggered by the conflict will transmit to regional inflation while simultaneously weakening consumption. Coupled with increased global economic uncertainty, the decision-making process for monetary policy normalization by regional central banks will become more complex. Central banks in some economies with weaker growth momentum and higher inflation sensitivity to energy prices will face particularly difficult trade-offs. The pandemic also serves as a reminder that regional economies need to rebuild a more sustainable and resilient growth model in the long term to prepare for other risks such as climate change. To this end, investors need to place greater emphasis on Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) factors in their investment considerations. Feature 2 examines whether stock market returns are affected by changes in climate risk, and how such sensitivity is influenced by corporate environmental performance. The novel coronavirus pandemic caused a huge shock to global financial markets in March 2020. During this period of market turbulence, some open-ended funds experienced significant outflows (Figure B1.1), placing pressure on their liquidity management. Figure B1.1 Fund Outflows from Some Open-Ended Funds During the March 2020 Event. Apart from investor liquidity needs, another reason for the large outflows may be that investors adopted a "first-mover advantage" to redeem funds early, thereby avoiding bearing redemption costs that could surge under market stress. To curb outflows induced by the first-mover advantage, some open-ended funds employ swing pricing—a pricing rule for open-ended funds designed to reduce the first-mover advantage for investors. Although many open-ended funds used swing pricing during this event, there is no empirical research indicating whether swing pricing can effectively reduce outflows from open-ended funds. Against this backdrop, this feature conducts empirical research to understand whether swing pricing was able to reduce fund outflows from open-ended funds during the March 2020 event, thereby reducing their liquidity risks. Additionally, this feature will identify factors that may limit the effectiveness of swing pricing during market stress. Based on these assessments, we will propose policy recommendations regarding financial stability. The first-mover advantage refers to investors redeeming before other investors, thereby shifting redemption costs onto them. The first-mover advantage primarily exists in open-ended funds using traditional pricing rules, where the subscription and redemption costs of fund investors (such as trading costs arising from portfolio adjustments) are reflected in the open-ended fund price after the transaction is executed. Under this pricing mechanism, investors who redeem shares first do not bear these trading costs. This becomes an incentive for them to redeem funds early, especially when large redemption costs are expected. Therefore, under market stress, the first-mover advantage becomes more pronounced due to the expectation of rising redemption costs. This amplifies the redemption pressure and liquidity risks faced by open-ended funds.

Driven by sustained growth in goods exports and private consumption, Hong Kong's economy continued its recovery in the second half of 2021, recording positive full-year growth for the first time since 2019. As 2022 commenced, a new wave of local infections and the resulting tightening of social distancing measures exerted pressure on local economic activity. Overall economic activity is projected to maintain a recovery throughout 2022, although the strength and pace of this recovery will be influenced by uncertainties and risks such as the pandemic and the normalization of US monetary policy. These adverse factors may also affect the outlook for the labor market, which had improved significantly in 2021. Although local inflation may rise slightly in the short term due to higher import prices, weak local rents and subdued labor costs should contain overall price pressures.  Hong Kong's economy continued its recovery in the second half of 2021. On a year-on-year basis, real Gross Local Product (GLP) grew by a further 5.5% in the third quarter and 4.8% in the fourth quarter (Table 3.A), albeit at a slower pace than in the first half of the year. For the full year of 2021, real GLP expanded by 6.4%, marking the first positive full-year growth since 2021. Figure 3.1 Real GLP Growth Rate and Contributions by Major Expenditure Components. On a quarter-on-quarter basis, economic activity recorded moderate growth of 0.6% and 0.2% in the third and fourth quarters of 2021, respectively (Figure 3.1). Domestically, an improving labor market, coupled with the government's consumption voucher scheme, propelled a rise in private consumption. However, overall investment spending moderated in the final quarter following two consecutive quarters of strong rebound. Externally, amid the continued global economic recovery, Hong Kong's goods trade performance remained robust, while services trade stayed weak, partly due to the stagnant tourism sector (Figure 3.2). On a net basis, external trade weighed on GLP in the third quarter but supported GLP growth in the fourth quarter. Figure 3.2 Volume of Imports and Exports.  A new wave of local infections and the consequent tightening of social distancing measures exerted pressure on Hong Kong's economic activity in early 2022. The government launched the fifth and sixth rounds of the Anti-Epidemic Fund and introduced additional counter-cyclical measures under the 2022-23 Budget to support the economy. To bolster cash flow, the "100% Guaranteed Personal Special Loan" and various guarantee products under the "SME Financing Guarantee Scheme" will be optimized, with higher maximum loan amounts, extended application periods, and longer repayment tenors. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA), together with the banking sector, has also extended the "Pre-approved Interest-only Repayment" scheme until the end of October 2022. The scheme will simultaneously offer borrowers a one-year partial principal repayment option, which will also apply to loans under the "SME Financing Guarantee Scheme."  It is projected that Hong Kong's economy will continue to recover over the full year of 2022, but the growth pace will be slower than in 2021, partly reflecting a slowdown in global economic growth amid the ongoing pandemic and higher base effects. Specifically, Hong Kong's goods exports are expected to continue benefiting from global economic expansion. Government promotion of various major infrastructure projects will also provide support to the economy. The government forecasts real GLP growth for 2022 to range between 2.0% and 3.5%, while the average growth forecast from international organizations and private sector analysts stands at 1.6%. However, the strength and pace of Hong Kong's economic recovery remain subject to numerous uncertainties and risks outlined in previous chapters. In particular, recent developments in the pandemic, an accelerated pace of US monetary policy normalization, and heightened geopolitical concerns (such as the situation in Ukraine) have cast a shadow over the near-term economic outlook for Hong Kong and the global economy. On the other hand, an earlier-than-expected resumption of quarantine-free travel between Hong Kong and mainland China could stimulate local economic growth.  With economic recovery, the labor market improved further in the second half of 2021, with the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate falling to 3.9% by year-end (Figure 3.3). Total employment in December 2021 also rebounded by 2.0% from the recent low in February 2021, though it remained below pre-pandemic levels. In early 2022, official data indicated that labor market pressures resurfaced amid the new wave of local infections. Additionally, a decline in the number of online job advertisements reflected a reduction in new job vacancies. Looking ahead, the new wave of local infections and tightened epidemic control measures are expected to exert some pressure on the local labor market in the short term, particularly in sectors involving face-to-face contact. In the longer term, the condition of the labor market will depend on the development of the local pandemic and the pace of economic recovery. Figure 3.3 Labor Market Conditions.  Local inflationary pressures have increased moderately in recent months but remain contained. On a year-on-year basis, the core consumer price inflation rate rose slightly to 1.1% and 1.2% in the third and fourth quarters of 2021, respectively, and remained at 1.2% in January 2022 (Figure 3.4). The annualized three-month core inflation rate, which reflects inflationary momentum, has also rebounded in recent months. Specifically, prices for dining out and some energy-related items have risen at an accelerated pace, driven by recovering domestic demand and higher external prices (Figure 3.5). Meanwhile, the housing rent component of the Comprehensive Consumer Price Index (CCPI) continued to decline broadly, thereby dampening overall inflationary momentum (Figure 3.6). Although real unit labor costs remain subdued, they have risen slightly in recent quarters, partly due to an improvement in real average wages (Figure 3.7). Figure 3.4 Various Indicators Reflecting Consumer Price Inflation. Figure 3.5 Hong Kong Import Prices. Figure 3.6 CCPI Rent Component and Market Rents. Figure 3.7 Unit Labor Costs.  Looking ahead, local inflation is expected to rise slightly in the short term due to rising import prices and logistics disruptions caused by the pandemic. However, weak rents and moderate local labor cost pressures should contain overall price pressures. Market consensus forecasts overall inflation for 2022 to reach 2.4%, while the government projects overall inflation at 2.1% and core inflation at 2.0% for 2022.

Amid risk-averse sentiment in the local equity market and concerns over the normalization of US monetary policy, the HKD exchange rate weakened during the review period. Given ample HKD liquidity, the Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate (HIBOR) remained at low levels. Overall, transactions in the HKD foreign exchange and money markets continued to proceed smoothly and in an orderly manner. Looking ahead, while uncertainties regarding US monetary policy, the pandemic, and escalating geopolitical tensions may exacerbate volatility in capital flows, Hong Kong's ample foreign exchange reserves and sound banking system enable it to withstand the shocks arising from such volatility. Overall, the HKD remained near the strong-side conversion band for most of the time, with trading continuing smoothly and in an orderly manner. Since September 2021, the HKD/USD exchange rate has gradually weakened amid risk-averse sentiment in the local equity market (Figure 4.1). Although the HKD rebounded slightly in October 2021 due to an improvement in market sentiment, the upward momentum subsequently faded, primarily owing to weak net southbound inflows via the Stock Connect schemes (Figure 4.2), as well as market expectations that the US dollar would strengthen as the Federal Reserve's monetary policy outlook turned more hawkish. During the review period, initial public offering (IPO) fundraising activities continued to provide support for the HKD (Figure 4.3). Total deposits grew moderately during the review period, with no significant signs of capital outflows from the local banking system. Meanwhile, the latest balance of payments data indicate that non-resident direct investment continued to flow into Hong Kong in the second half of 2021, and there were no indications of abnormal cross-border capital flows. Figure 4.1: HKD exchange rate. Figure 4.2: Net southbound purchases via the Shanghai-HK Stock Connect and Shenzhen-HK Stock Connect. Figure 4.3: Equity funds raised on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange (HKEX). Although the US dollar strengthened during the review period, the HKD nominal effective exchange rate index remained stable due to the appreciation of the RMB against the HKD (Figure 4.4). Given the small inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners, the HKD real effective exchange rate index broadly followed the trend of the nominal effective exchange rate index. Figure 4.4: Nominal and real effective exchange rates. Looking ahead, uncertainties regarding US monetary policy, the evolution of the pandemic, and escalating geopolitical tensions may exacerbate volatility in capital flows. As US interest rates rise, under the normal operation of the Linked Exchange Rate System (LERS), an outflow of HKD funds (the speed and scale of which will depend on prevailing market conditions at the time) could lead to a weakening of the HKD and trigger the weak-side conversion guarantee. Hong Kong also possesses ample foreign exchange reserves and a sound banking system, enabling it to withstand capital flow volatility without compromising financial stability. During the review period, Hong Kong's monetary environment remained accommodative. The HKD monetary base increased by 1.4% over the eight months since the end of June 2021, primarily driven by an increase in Certificates of Indebtedness (CDIs). Reflecting the continued demand for Exchange Fund Bills and Notes (EFBNs) by banks to meet their liquidity needs in a liquid banking system, EFBNs outstanding increased by HK$119.7 billion to HK$1,188.7 billion during the review period, while the total balance (before Discount Window operations) correspondingly decreased by HK$119.9 billion to HK$337.6 billion (Figure 4.5). Meanwhile, the amount of banknotes and coins issued by the government remained relatively stable. Figure 4.5: Total balance and Exchange Fund Bills and Notes. Over the six months since the end of July 2021, total deposits at authorized institutions grew moderately by 4.5%, while HKD deposits increased slightly by 0.3%. However, it should be noted that monetary statistics may be subject to fluctuations due to various short-term factors (such as seasonal and IPO-related funding needs, as well as business and investment-related activities); therefore, it is appropriate to observe longer-term trends. For the full year of 2021, total deposits and HKD deposits increased by 4.6% and 1.4%, respectively. Figure 4.6: Deposits at authorized institutions by currency. Overall, transactions in Hong Kong's interbank market continued to proceed smoothly and in an orderly manner. Given ample liquidity in the banking system, HIBOR remained at low levels despite market concerns over tightening US monetary policy (Figure 4.7). Partially reflecting market expectations of rising funding demand toward year-end, HIBOR edged up slightly in December 2021. The average mortgage lending rate for new loans rose slightly from 1.48% in July 2021 to 1.56% in January 2022. On the other hand, the prime lending rates of major retail banks remained unchanged during the review period, ranging between 5.00% and 5.50%. Looking ahead, ample liquidity in the banking system will provide sufficient buffers in the event of major capital market activities or financial market volatility. Figure 4.7: HIBOR and USD HIBOR. During the review period, the offshore RMB interbank market continued to function normally. Affected by seasonal liquidity demand toward year-end, the overnight offshore RMB HIBOR experienced slight volatility in late December 2021, while the three-month offshore RMB HIBOR remained relatively stable, hovering around 3% throughout the review period (Figure 4.8). Figure 4.8: Overnight and three-month offshore RMB HIBOR pricing. In the second half of 2021, Hong Kong's offshore RMB pool continued to grow steadily. Over the six months since the end of July 2021, the balance of RMB customer deposits and certificates of deposit increased by 30.3%, reaching RMB 1.1135 trillion by the end of January 2022 (Figure 4.9 and Table 4.A). Among these, RMB customer deposits increased by 33.5%, mainly driven by corporate fund inflows, offsetting a 48.0% decline in the balance of certificates of deposit. Figure 4.9: RMB deposits and certificates of deposit in Hong Kong. Over the six-month period since July 2021, although the balance of RMB loans decreased by 10.2% to RMB 167.6 billion, RMB trade settlement in Hong Kong continued to grow. Between the end of July 2021 and the end of January 2022, local banks processed transactions totaling RMB 3.763 trillion (Figure 4.10), an increase of 18.3% compared to RMB 3.181 trillion in the same period last year. Hong Kong's substantial RMB pool continues to support a large volume of RMB payment and financing transactions. For the full year of 2021, the average daily turnover of the RMB Real-Time Gross Settlement (RTGS) system increased from RMB 1.1915 trillion in 2020 to RMB 1.5226 trillion. Figure 4.10: RMB trade settlement remittances. Looking ahead, Hong Kong's offshore RMB business is expected to benefit from the establishment of the northbound and southbound channels under the Stock Connect, Bond Connect, and Cross-Bay Wealth Management Connect schemes, the continued opening of the mainland's capital account, increasing demand from international investors for RMB assets, and the deepening of regional economic and financial cooperation under the Belt and Road Initiative and the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area initiative. Global major stock markets continued to rise in the fourth quarter of 2021, but amid growing concerns over the tightening stance of major central banks in advanced economies and the escalating conflict between Russia and Ukraine, major stock markets have consolidated since January 2022. The Hong Kong stock market remained subdued in the fourth quarter of 2021, primarily dragged down by a sharp decline in technology stocks. Global risks and uncertainties surrounding the evolution of the pandemic in Hong Kong caused the Hang Seng Index (HSI) to fall to a near two-year low by the end of February. Meanwhile, Hong Kong's offshore RMB bond market continued to grow steadily in the second half of 2021. The residential property market has softened since mid-2021, partly due to a weakening sentiment in asset markets and a new wave of the local pandemic. Global major stock markets continued to rise overall in the last quarter of 2021, driving the Morgan Stanley Capital International (MSCI) World Index to a record high of 3,262 points on January 4, 2022 (Figure 4.11). The recovery of the global economy and strong corporate earnings, supported by government monetary and fiscal policies, underpinned the upward trend in global major stock markets, though the pandemic remained the primary risk concern for investors throughout the year. However, global major stock markets have consolidated since early January 2022, amid growing concerns over the tightening stance of major central banks in advanced economies in the face of surging inflation risks, soaring commodity prices, and the escalating Russia-Ukraine conflict. In contrast, by the end of 2021, the Hong Kong stock market continued to lag behind other global major stock markets. The HSI hovered between 24,000 and 26,500 points from September to mid-November, closing at 23,398 points at the end of 2021, a decline of 14.1% from 2020. In early 2022, buying interest from value investors returned to the Hong Kong stock market, pushing the HSI back to around 25,000 points in January. However, uncertainties surrounding the evolution of the pandemic in Hong Kong and the escalating Russia-Ukraine conflict dragged the HSI down to a near two-year low of 22,713 points by the end of February. Over the entire review period from the end of August 2021 to February 2022, the HSI fell by 12.2%, while the MSCI World Index declined by 5.2% (Figure 4.11). Figure 4.11: Hang Seng Index and MSCI World Index. The implied volatility of the stock market surged sharply in late November 2021 due to the emergence of the highly transmissible Omicron variant, before subsequently receding. Although the skew index retreated from its historical high in late June 2021, it remained elevated, reflecting investors' concerns that the long-term rebound in equity markets since the outbreak of the pandemic may be subject to correction, thus prompting them to allocate more funds to hedge against downside equity risk (Figure 4.12). Figure 4.12: Option implied volatility of the Hang Seng Index and S&P 500 Index, and the skew index. Against the backdrop of ample global liquidity, Hong Kong stocks have continued to record net inflows from international investors since the last report (Figure 4.13). In contrast, the southbound channel under the Stock Connect recorded significant net outflows in the third quarter of 2021, primarily due to concerns over the impact of regulatory changes in the mainland on technology stocks. However, southbound buying via the Stock Connect began to recover in December 2021, with cumulative net inflows reaching HK$98.3 billion by the end of February. During the review period, the cumulative net purchase amount increased by 5.7% to HK$2.233 trillion (Figure 4.14). Figure 4.13: Net capital flows in Hong Kong's stock market. Figure 4.14: Net flows via the Stock Connect mechanism. After setting a record high in the first half of 2021, fundraising in Hong Kong's primary market slowed in the second half. For the full year of 2021, there were 98 new listings, raising a total of HK$328.9 billion (Figure 4.15), representing a 17.8% decline compared to the previous year. In 2021, the HKEX ranked fourth globally in the IPO market, trailing only the NASDAQ, the New York Stock Exchange, and the Shanghai Stock Exchange. Figure 4.15: Hong Kong IPO market. The outlook for the local stock market remains uncertain. A relaxation of mainland monetary policy and more Chinese concept stocks listing secondarily in Hong Kong's primary market will improve sentiment in the Hong Kong stock market. However, the stock market still faces many adverse factors, including uncertainties surrounding the evolution of the pandemic in Hong Kong, a faster-than-expected pace of normalization of US monetary policy, and the escalation of the Russia-Ukraine conflict.

The profitability of Hong Kong's retail banks declined in the second half of 2021. The specific classification loan ratio rose slightly in the second half of 2021 but remained at low levels by both historical and international standards. Underpinned by sound capital and liquidity positions, the Hong Kong banking sector remained resilient. During the review period, the HKMA continued multiple support measures to further assist the economy in navigating difficult times. Looking ahead, the rapid spread of the Omicron variant may pose a threat to economic recovery, and the risk that the pace of US monetary policy normalization may be faster than expected; together, these factors will challenge banks' credit risk management. Banks should remain vigilant and carefully assess the potential impact of these risk factors on the asset quality of their loan portfolios. In the second half of 2021, the overall pre-tax operating profit of retail banks fell by 16.1% compared with the same period in 2020. Weak profitability was primarily attributable to declines in net interest and non-interest income, coupled with increased operating expenses. Consequently, the return on assets (ROA) declined to 0.50% in the second half of 2021, from 0.61% in the same period of 2020 (Figure 5.1). For the full year 2021, the overall pre-tax operating profit of retail banks decreased by 18.6% compared with 2020, while ROA declined from 0.77% to 0.59%. Figure 5.1: Retail Bank Profitability. The profitability of retail banks reflects the continuing impact of the low-interest environment, with the net interest margin (NIM) of retail banks remaining at a low level of 0.98% in the second half of 2021 (Figure 5.2). Figure 5.2: Net Interest Margin of Retail Banks. The NIM of retail banks reflected year-end funding needs and the decline in the HKMA's total outstanding balance following the issuance of additional Exchange Fund Bills. As a result, the Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate (HIBOR) recorded a slight increase in the last quarter of 2021. However, given that liquidity in the banking system remained very ample, HIBOR continued to remain at relatively low levels. Specifically, the 3-month HIBOR rose slightly by 9 basis points from six months earlier to 0.26% at the end of December 2021 (see the blue line in Figure 5.3). The funding costs of retail banks remained stable during the review period. In particular, the composite rate (an indicator measuring the average Hong Kong dollar funding cost of retail banks) rose moderately by 3 basis points from 0.18% six months earlier to 0.21% at the end of 2021 (the green line in Figure 5.3). Climate change affects every aspect of life, and everyone has a responsibility to contribute to mitigating its impacts. In this regard, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) has dedicated significant efforts to advancing Hong Kong's climate goals and enhancing global climate resilience and sustainable development. Following the inclusion of our first Sustainability Report as a chapter in the HKMA's 2021 Annual Report last year, we are publishing the 2022 Sustainability Report as a standalone document for the first time this year. I hope this report will enable readers to gain a deeper understanding of the HKMA's strategic priorities and key initiatives in strengthening the Hong Kong banking system's capacity to address climate change, building a green finance ecosystem, and fulfilling our roles as a responsible investor and a sustainable development institution. Over the past year, we have made significant progress in advancing sustainability across the HKMA's core functions. This report details our specific measures and activities, with particular emphasis on the following key areas: Banks face climate risks in their daily operations. As the banking regulator, the HKMA has taken concrete steps to enhance banks' capacity to respond to climate change. In 2022, we launched a two-year plan to integrate climate risk factors into our supervisory framework and are exploring how technology can assist banks in assessing the impacts of physical risks. Recognizing the growing number of green and sustainable products launched by banks, we have also shared best practices with the industry on effectively managing these products to strengthen banks' climate risk management capabilities. The HKMA actively participates in various collaborative initiatives aimed at addressing climate risks and promoting the development of sustainable finance. Locally, we are working with other financial regulators through the "Cross-Sectoral Steering Committee on Green and Sustainable Finance" (Steering Committee) to develop a local green taxonomy framework. This framework will enhance transparency in financial markets and promote greater consistency in green finance policies. Internationally, we are actively engaged with multiple international organizations to assist in formulating climate change policies and assessing their impacts on financial stability. Hong Kong is well-positioned to meet Asia's demand for green and sustainable financing. Despite 2022 being a particularly challenging year for the global bond market, Hong Kong continued to record strong growth in green and sustainable debt issuance, with a 42% increase, bringing the total issuance to USD 80.5 billion. This reaffirms Hong Kong's status as Asia's largest hub for arranging international green and sustainable bond issuances. Relevant issuers included the governments of Shenzhen and Hainan provinces, whose issuances once again demonstrate Hong Kong's unique role in facilitating the flow of green and sustainable capital between Mainland China and international markets. The robust development of Hong Kong's green bond market is partly attributable to the Government Green Bond Programme. Since 2019, the HKMA has assisted the government in issuing green bonds totaling nearly USD 16 billion. The proceeds have been allocated to over 40 green government projects, including green buildings, waste management and recycling, energy efficiency, and energy conservation. We also assisted the government in achieving two "firsts": in May 2022, we helped issue the first batch of government green retail bonds worth HKD 20 billion, which was the largest green retail bond issuance globally at the time. Additionally, in February 2023, we assisted in the issuance of the first batch of tokenized green bonds. These were the world's first tokenized green bonds issued by a government, marking a milestone that successfully combines our strengths in the bond market, green and sustainable finance, and fintech. Standards, data, and talent are indispensable elements for fostering a healthy climate finance ecosystem and require concerted efforts and collaboration across different sectors. To this end, the HKMA primarily collaborates with other relevant government departments, regulators, academic institutions, and the financial industry through the Steering Committee to develop these elements. In addition to developing the local green taxonomy framework as mentioned above, the Steering Committee, through its established "Centre for Green and Sustainable Finance," promotes skills training within the industry and improves Hong Kong's data resources. Furthermore, the Steering Committee has made good progress in other areas, including mandatory disclosure of climate-related information and opportunities in carbon markets. In 2022, the HKMA further strengthened the Exchange Fund's work on responsible investment, notably by setting a target for the Exchange Fund's investment portfolio to achieve net-zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050. Concurrently, we have optimized risk management practices to enhance the Exchange Fund's climate resilience and risk-adjusted long-term returns. Moreover, to fully capitalize on potential opportunities arising from climate change, we are committed to promoting sustainable investments by the Exchange Fund, identifying investment opportunities that support climate transition and mitigation to enhance long-term portfolio returns. By the end of 2021, the weighted average carbon intensity of the Exchange Fund's equity portfolio had decreased by 43% compared to 2017 levels. In fact, the Exchange Fund's exposure to high-carbon assets has consistently remained lower than that of the broader market. Looking ahead, we will continue to advance toward the net-zero target by continuously integrating environmental, social, and governance (ESG) factors into the investment management process, actively exercising asset ownership, maintaining ongoing collaboration with stakeholders, and focusing on decarbonization and transition within the portfolio. At the HKMA, the "Institutional Social Responsibility and Sustainability Committee," chaired by me, is responsible for formulating the HKMA's sustainability strategy. Our strategic direction is built upon three pillars: the environment, employees, and social responsibility. Regarding the environment, we are committed to promoting a green workplace and advocating for a more environmentally friendly market to the public. Concerning employees, as a responsible and caring employer, we actively cultivate a healthy and inclusive work environment. In terms of social responsibility, we strive to enhance public financial literacy, promote financial inclusion, and actively give back to society. Compared to our baseline levels when we began tracking our carbon footprint in 2015, our per capita greenhouse gas emissions, energy consumption, and paper usage in 2022 all achieved double-digit reductions. More importantly, we have formulated a roadmap to achieve net-zero emissions by 2050 or earlier. In the short term, our goals are to completely eliminate Scope 1 emissions and reduce Scope 2 emissions by 63% by 2030 or earlier, using 2015 as the baseline. Addressing climate change and promoting sustainable development require continuous efforts and collaboration from multiple parties. On this critical global issue, we understand the necessity of leading by example and working together with like-minded industry peers and international organizations. The next section will outline the HKMA's short-term plans and key priorities for addressing climate change under its major functions. Achieving net-zero emissions by 2050 or earlier is a formidable task, and we will spare no effort to realize this goal. We are confident that, through the joint efforts of all our staff, the financial industry, and the general public, we will successfully meet future climate challenges.  Chief Executive, Wilson YU

In 2023, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) will continue to promote sustainable development within Hong Kong's financial sector and fulfill its responsibilities as a responsible investor and a sustainable institution. At the same time, through participation in international and regional organizations, the HKMA will also be committed to promoting the broad development and best practices of green and sustainable finance. As the banking regulator, we will strive to enhance the climate resilience of the banking sector and further improve our green finance ecosystem to support banks' green transformation. Specifically, the HKMA will engage with banks to understand their progress in implementing regulatory requirements on climate risk management, incorporate climate factors into our supervisory review processes, and revise the banking sector's "Green Benchmarks" common assessment framework. Meanwhile, the HKMA will support banks' efforts to enhance their climate resilience and risk management capabilities, for example by exploring various measures and technological solutions to assist banks in identifying, measuring, and monitoring their climate risk exposures. The HKMA will also collaborate with banks to conduct the next round of climate risk stress tests as part of the regulator-led periodic stress tests for the 2023–2024 financial year. Participating banks will be required to assess their capacity to respond to climate risks based on an optimized stress testing framework that covers multiple stress scenarios, including extreme climate events and adverse economic conditions. To foster healthy development in banks' provision of green and sustainable investment products, the HKMA will closely monitor local and international market and regulatory developments, maintain communication with the industry, and provide timely guidance on sales processes. We will also conduct off-site thematic assessments to gain a comprehensive understanding of the green and sustainable investment products offered by banks. Concurrently, to strengthen the construction of a green finance ecosystem supporting the green transformation of the financial sector, the HKMA is planning to consult the industry on the structure and core elements of a local green taxonomy framework. In terms of market development, to promote Hong Kong as a regional hub for green and sustainable finance, the HKMA will assist the government in expanding the issuance scale of green bonds under the "Government Green Bond Scheme" and broaden the scheme's scope to include sustainability bonds; at the same time, through the "Green and Sustainable Finance Fund," it will attract more green financing activities to take place in Hong Kong. The HKMA is also assisting in the implementation of the government-funded "Green and Sustainable Finance Training Pilot Scheme" to expand Hong Kong's talent pool in green finance. In addition, the HKMA will continue to encourage more mainland local governments, institutions, and enterprises to conduct green financing through Hong Kong, and explore the feasibility of integrating green finance with technology. On the other hand, we will continue to collaborate with other institutional departments through the "Green and Sustainable Finance Cross-Institutional Steering Group" on cross-industry issues such as skills training and data, green taxonomies, climate-related disclosures and sustainability reporting, and carbon market opportunities. Through the Green Banking Alliance, the HKMA will jointly launch various targeted initiatives with the International Finance Corporation in the Asia region, including conducting green finance research, providing unique market analysis, offering targeted professional training for banks, and supplying practical guidelines to assist banks in developing roadmaps to make green finance a core business. Looking ahead, the Alliance will work closely with its founding members, global partners, and knowledge partners to launch a membership program to expand the Alliance's influence in the Asia region. At the same time, the Alliance will also strengthen the professional capabilities of industry practitioners, promote knowledge sharing in green finance, and lead the launch of project initiatives in new areas.
